fragments.text: Height per unit x; it can exceed 1 provided areas are valid probabilities.

fragments.label: Median
fragments.text: A value m with equal probability on either side for a continuous distribution.

fragments.label: Support
fragments.text: The interval on which the density is non-zero.
Valid density functions

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A pdf f(x) must satisfy f(x)≥0 on its support and ∫f(x)dx=1 over the whole support. Use normalisation to find unknown constants, checking they keep the density non-negative.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: A density value is not itself a point probability.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Outside the stated support, f(x)=0.

fragments.label: Valid density functions
fragments.text: Normalisation: ∫ f(x) dx=1 over the support
Probabilities as areas

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: P(a < X < b)=∫ₐᵇf(x)dx after intersecting the requested interval with the support. For continuous X, endpoints make no difference: P(X=a)=0.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Draw the support and shade the required interval.

fragments.label: Probabilities as areas
fragments.text: Use complements for awkward tails.
Percentiles

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: A pth percentile q satisfies ∫ from the lower support limit to q of f(x)dx=p/100. The median uses 0.5. Solve and select the root that lies within the support.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Do not assume median equals mean unless symmetry justifies it.

fragments.label: Percentiles
fragments.text: Reject algebraic roots outside the support.
Moments

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Calculate E(X)=∫xf(x)dx and E(X²)=∫x²f(x)dx over the support, then Var(X)=E(X²)−[E(X)]². Interpret the mean in the same units as X and variance in squared units.

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Normalise before calculating moments.

fragments.label: Moments
fragments.text: Keep exact values until the variance subtraction is complete.
Can a pdf exceed 1?

fragments.label: Can a pdf exceed 1?
fragments.text: Yes; only areas must be between 0 and 1, and total area must equal 1.
What is P(X=a) for continuous X?

fragments.label: What is P(X=a) for continuous X?
fragments.text: Zero.
How is the median found?

fragments.label: How is the median found?
fragments.text: Set the area from the lower support boundary to m equal to 0.5.
Which root of a percentile equation is valid?

fragments.label: Which root of a percentile equation is valid?
fragments.text: Only a root lying in the stated support.

Understand sampling distributions and construct confidence intervals to estimate an unknown population parameter. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Population
fragments.text: The full set about which an inference is made.

fragments.label: Sample
fragments.text: A subset observed to learn about the population.

fragments.label: Sampling distribution
fragments.text: The probability distribution of a statistic over repeated samples.

fragments.label: Standard error
fragments.text: The standard deviation of a sampling distribution.

fragments.label: Confidence interval
fragments.text: A range generated by a method that captures the true parameter at a stated long-run rate.
Random samples and bias

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Every population member should have an appropriate chance of selection. Convenience, voluntary-response and incomplete-frame samples can be biased. Random numbers help choose units without personal judgement.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: A large biased sample is still biased.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Distinguish sampling variation from measurement error.

fragments.label: Random samples and bias
fragments.text: Sample mean moments: E(X̄)=μ; Var(X̄)=σ²/n
Sample mean distribution

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: If population mean is μ and variance σ², then E(X̄)=μ and Var(X̄)=σ²/n. X̄ is normal if the population is normal and approximately normal for large n by the CLT.

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: Standard error is σ/√n.

fragments.label: Sample mean distribution
fragments.text: Increasing n reduces standard error by the square-root law.
Unbiased estimates

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Estimate μ by x̄. Estimate population variance with s²=Σ(x−x̄)²/(n−1), equivalently [Σx²−(Σx)²/n]/(n−1). The n−1 correction makes the estimating process unbiased.

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Use the sample variance requested, not the descriptive variance with denominator n.

fragments.label: Unbiased estimates
fragments.text: Keep x̄ unrounded in the variance formula.
Confidence intervals

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: For known σ or a large sample, a confidence interval for μ is x̄±z*σ/√n, replacing σ by s for a large sample when needed. For a large-sample proportion p, use p̂±z*√[p̂(1−p̂)/n]. Interpret the confidence level as a property of the method.

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: 90%, 95%, 99% use different central z-values.

fragments.label: Confidence intervals
fragments.text: Give interval endpoints in context and sensible units.
What is the standard error of X̄?

fragments.label: What is the standard error of X̄?
fragments.text: σ/√n.
Why is n−1 used in the sample variance?

fragments.label: Why is n−1 used in the sample variance?
fragments.text: It corrects the systematic underestimation and makes the estimator unbiased.
What does a 95% confidence method mean?

fragments.label: What does a 95% confidence method mean?
fragments.text: Across repeated samples, about 95% of intervals produced by the method contain the true parameter.
What happens to standard error if n is quadrupled?

fragments.label: What happens to standard error if n is quadrupled?
fragments.text: It is halved.

Set up null and alternative hypotheses, use a critical region or p-value, and draw a conclusion in the context of the question. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.

fragments.label: Null hypothesis
fragments.text: H₀, the model or parameter value tested as the default claim.

fragments.label: Alternative hypothesis
fragments.text: H₁, the direction or difference supported if H₀ is rejected.

fragments.label: Significance level
fragments.text: The maximum chosen probability of rejecting H₀ when it is true.

fragments.label: Critical region
fragments.text: Test-statistic values that lead to rejection of H₀.

fragments.label: p-value
fragments.text: The probability under H₀ of an outcome at least as extreme as observed in the direction(s) of H₁.

fragments.label: Type I error
fragments.text: Rejecting a true H₀.

fragments.label: Type II error
fragments.text: Failing to reject a false H₀ under a specified alternative.
Setting up the test

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Define the parameter, write H₀ with equality, and make H₁ match the claim. 'Increased' gives an upper tail, 'decreased' a lower tail, and 'changed' two tails. The test calculation always uses the H₀ parameter.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Use population parameters, not sample statistics, in hypotheses.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Choose the tail before seeing the result.

fragments.label: Setting up the test
fragments.text: Mean test statistic: Z=(X̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n)
Discrete tests

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: For X binomial or Poisson, find the probability of the observed result or something more extreme under H₀. Reject if that p-value is ≤α. A critical region is chosen so its H₀ probability is at most α; discreteness means the actual size may be smaller.

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: For two tails, identify both extremes rather than blindly doubling if the distribution is asymmetric.

fragments.label: Discrete tests
fragments.text: State the actual critical-region probability when requested.
Normal and mean tests

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: Use a continuity-corrected normal approximation for binomial/Poisson when conditions hold. For a mean, standardise Z=(X̄−μ₀)/(σ/√n), using s for σ in a large-sample setting as allowed, then compare with the relevant critical value or p-value.

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: Put μ₀ from H₀ in the numerator.

fragments.label: Normal and mean tests
fragments.text: A two-tailed α test places α/2 in each tail.
Errors and conclusions

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: Type I probability is the rejection-region probability under H₀. Type II probability is the acceptance-region probability under a specified alternative. Finish with 'reject H₀' or 'do not reject H₀', followed by a contextual evidence statement—never say H₀ is proved.

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: Power=1−P(Type II error).

fragments.label: Errors and conclusions
fragments.text: The conclusion must use the direction in H₁.
Where does equality belong in hypotheses?

fragments.label: Where does equality belong in hypotheses?
fragments.text: In H₀.
What tail matches 'the mean has decreased'?

fragments.label: What tail matches 'the mean has decreased'?
fragments.text: A lower-tailed test.
What is a Type I error?

fragments.label: What is a Type I error?
fragments.text: Rejecting H₀ when H₀ is true.
How should a non-significant result be stated?

fragments.label: How should a non-significant result be stated?
fragments.text: Do not reject H₀; there is insufficient evidence for the contextual alternative claim.

Everything a computer stores is a pattern of bits, so Paper 1 repeatedly asks you to convert between number bases, represent negative numbers in two's complement, add binary values and spot overflow. Questions also test binary versus decimal prefixes, BCD and character sets, usually with a short justification of why one representation suits a given use.

fragments.label: Bit
fragments.text: A binary digit, 0 or 1; the smallest unit of data a computer stores.

fragments.label: Byte
fragments.text: A group of 8 bits, treated as a single unit of storage.

fragments.label: Binary prefix
fragments.text: A multiplier based on powers of 2, such as kibi (2^10 = 1024), mebi (2^20) and gibi (2^30).

fragments.label: Decimal prefix
fragments.text: A multiplier based on powers of 10, such as kilo (10^3 = 1000), mega (10^6) and giga (10^9).

fragments.label: Hexadecimal
fragments.text: A base-16 number system using the digits 0–9 and A–F; each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits.

fragments.label: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)
fragments.text: A representation in which each denary digit is stored separately as its own 4-bit binary code (a nibble).

fragments.label: One's complement
fragments.text: A signed representation in which a negative number is formed by inverting every bit of the positive value.

fragments.label: Two's complement
fragments.text: A signed representation in which the most significant bit has a negative place value; a negative is formed by inverting all bits of the positive value and adding 1.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: The error that occurs when the result of a calculation is too large (or too small) to be represented in the available number of bits.

fragments.label: Character set
fragments.text: The complete list of characters a computer recognises, each paired with a unique binary code.
Binary magnitudes and prefixes

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Memory is addressed in powers of 2, so storage is naturally measured with binary prefixes: 1 kibibyte (KiB) = 2^10 = 1024 bytes, 1 mebibyte (MiB) = 2^20 bytes, 1 gibibyte (GiB) = 2^30 bytes and 1 tebibyte (TiB) = 2^40 bytes. Decimal prefixes follow the SI system: 1 kilobyte (kB) = 1000 bytes, 1 megabyte (MB) = 10^6 bytes, and so on. Storage manufacturers often use decimal prefixes, which is why a '500 GB' drive shows as roughly 465 GiB in an operating system.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Each step up a binary prefix multiplies by 1024; each step up a decimal prefix multiplies by 1000.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: The gap grows with size: 1 KiB is 2.4% larger than 1 kB, but 1 TiB is about 10% larger than 1 TB.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text: Use the prefix named in the question; if it says MiB, divide by 1024 twice, not by 1,000,000.

fragments.label: Binary magnitudes and prefixes
fragments.text:
3 MiB = 3 × 1024 × 1024 = 3,145,728 bytes.
3 MB = 3 × 1000 × 1000 = 3,000,000 bytes.
Difference = 145,728 bytes, so the binary-prefix value is larger.
Binary, denary and hexadecimal

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: In binary each column is worth double the one to its right (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 for a byte). To convert denary to binary, subtract the largest column values that fit, or divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders upwards. Hexadecimal groups binary into nibbles: split the binary into groups of 4 bits from the right and replace each group with one hex digit (10 = A, 11 = B … 15 = F).

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: Hex to denary: multiply each digit by its place value (16^1, 16^0) and add, e.g. 3F = 3 × 16 + 15 = 63.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: Always pad a nibble to 4 bits before converting to hex, e.g. 101 becomes 0101 = 5.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text: An n-bit unsigned binary integer can represent 0 to 2^n − 1, so a byte holds 0 to 255.

fragments.label: Binary, denary and hexadecimal
fragments.text:
181 − 128 = 53 → 1 in the 128 column
53 − 32 = 21 → 1 in the 32 column (0 in 64)
21 − 16 = 5 → 1 in the 16 column
5 − 4 = 1 → 1 in the 4 column (0 in 8)
1 − 1 = 0 → 1 in the 1 column (0 in 2)
Binary = 1011 0101
Hex: 1011 = B, 0101 = 5 → B5
Check: 11 × 16 + 5 = 181
Uses of hexadecimal and BCD

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal and BCD
fragments.text: Hexadecimal is used because it is shorter and less error-prone for humans to read than long binary strings, yet converts directly to binary. BCD stores each denary digit in its own nibble, so 395 becomes 0011 1001 0101 rather than the pure binary 110001011. BCD is less storage-efficient (the codes 1010–1111 are never used) but avoids conversion rounding and makes displaying digits simple.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal and BCD
fragments.text: Hex uses: memory addresses, MAC addresses, colour codes such as #FF8000, error codes and assembly/machine-code listings.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal and BCD
fragments.text: BCD uses: digital clocks and calculators driving seven-segment displays, and financial systems where exact denary values must be stored without rounding errors.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal and BCD
fragments.text: When justifying BCD, link it to each digit being processed or displayed separately.

fragments.label: Uses of hexadecimal and BCD
fragments.text:
Denary 395
3 → 0011
9 → 1001
5 → 0101
BCD = 0011 1001 0101 (12 bits)
Pure binary 395 = 1 1000 1011 (9 bits), showing BCD needs more space.
One's and two's complement

fragments.label: One's and two's complement
fragments.text: In two's complement the most significant bit has a negative place value (−128 in a byte), so 8 bits represent −128 to +127. To find the negative of a number, write the positive value, invert every bit (this gives the one's complement), then add 1. To read a two's complement value, add the negative MSB value to the positive values of the remaining 1 bits.

fragments.label: One's and two's complement
fragments.text: A leading 1 means the number is negative; a leading 0 means it is zero or positive.

fragments.label: One's and two's complement
fragments.text: One's complement has two representations of zero (00000000 and 11111111), which is one reason two's complement is preferred.

fragments.label: One's and two's complement
fragments.text: Two's complement lets the same adder circuit perform both addition and subtraction.

fragments.label: One's and two's complement
fragments.text: Range of n-bit two's complement: −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1.
Binary addition and subtraction

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Binary addition follows four rules: 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 0 carry 1, and 1 + 1 + 1 = 1 carry 1. Subtraction is performed by adding the two's complement of the number being subtracted, so A − B becomes A + (−B). Any carry out of the most significant bit is discarded in two's complement arithmetic.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Show carries above the columns; examiners award method marks for visible working.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Convert the answer back to denary to check it.

fragments.label: Binary addition and subtraction
fragments.text: Discarding the final carry is not the same as overflow; check the signs instead.
Overflow

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: Overflow happens when a result falls outside the range the register can hold. In two's complement it is detected when two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign: two positives giving a negative, or two negatives giving a positive. The processor records this in an overflow flag in the status register so software can react.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: Adding numbers of opposite signs can never overflow.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: With unsigned numbers, a carry out of the MSB indicates the result was too large.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text: Using more bits (for example 16 instead of 8) extends the range and makes overflow less likely.

fragments.label: Overflow
fragments.text:
0110 0100  (+100)
+ 0011 0010  (+50)
= 1001 0110
The correct answer is +150, which is above +127. The result's MSB is 1, so it reads as −128 + 16 + 4 + 2 = −106: two positives have produced a negative, so overflow has occurred.
Character sets

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Text is stored by giving each character a numeric code from a character set. Standard ASCII uses 7 bits, giving 128 codes covering English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters. Extended ASCII uses 8 bits for 256 codes, adding accented and graphical characters. Unicode uses up to 4 bytes per character so that characters from almost every writing system, plus symbols and emoji, can be represented, while its first 128 codes match ASCII.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Codes are allocated in sequence: 'A' = 65, 'B' = 66; 'a' = 97; the digit '0' = 48, so lower case is 32 more than upper case.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Because codes are sequential, strings can be sorted and compared by comparing their codes.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: Unicode needs more storage per character than ASCII but supports international text on one system.

fragments.label: Character sets
fragments.text: The character '7' (code 55) is different from the integer 7; converting between them is a common exam point.
How many bytes are in 1 KiB and in 1 kB?

fragments.label: How many bytes are in 1 KiB and in 1 kB?

fragments.text: What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?

fragments.label: What is the range of an 8-bit two's complement integer?

fragments.text: How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?

fragments.label: How do you find the two's complement of a negative number?
fragments.text: Write the positive value in binary, invert every bit, then add 1.
How is overflow detected when adding two's complement numbers?

fragments.label: How is overflow detected when adding two's complement numbers?
fragments.text: Two numbers of the same sign are added and the result has the opposite sign.
What is 0011 1001 in BCD?

fragments.label: What is 0011 1001 in BCD?
fragments.text: 39 — each nibble is one denary digit (3 and 9).
Give two uses of hexadecimal.

fragments.label: Give two uses of hexadecimal.
fragments.text: Any two of: memory addresses, MAC addresses, HTML colour codes, error codes, machine-code/assembly listings.
Why is Unicode needed when ASCII exists?

fragments.label: Why is Unicode needed when ASCII exists?
fragments.text: ASCII has only 128 (or 256 extended) codes, which cannot represent characters from all languages; Unicode can.
Why does one's complement have a disadvantage compared with two's complement?

fragments.label: Why does one's complement have a disadvantage compared with two's complement?
fragments.text: It has two representations of zero, and addition needs extra correction steps.

Images and sound must be turned into binary before a computer can store them. Paper 1 asks you to explain how bitmaps and vector graphics are encoded, calculate bitmap and sound file sizes, describe how changing resolution, colour depth, sampling rate or sampling resolution affects quality and size, and justify choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic for a given task.

fragments.label: Pixel
fragments.text: The smallest addressable element of a bitmap image; a single dot of one colour.

fragments.label: Image resolution
fragments.text: The number of pixels in an image, given as width × height (for example 1920 × 1080).

fragments.label: Screen resolution
fragments.text: The number of pixels a display screen can show horizontally and vertically.

fragments.label: Colour depth (bit depth)
fragments.text: The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel; n bits allow 2^n different colours.

fragments.label: File header
fragments.text: Data at the start of an image or sound file describing the file, such as its type, dimensions, colour depth or sampling rate.

fragments.label: Drawing object
fragments.text: A single shape in a vector graphic, such as a line, rectangle or circle.

fragments.label: Property
fragments.text: A value that defines how a drawing object looks, such as its coordinates, size, line colour, line width or fill colour.

fragments.label: Drawing list
fragments.text: The set of commands in a vector graphic file that define every drawing object and its properties.

fragments.label: Sampling rate
fragments.text: The number of samples of a sound wave's amplitude taken per second, measured in hertz (Hz).

fragments.label: Sampling resolution
fragments.text: The number of bits used to store each sound sample; it sets how many amplitude levels can be recorded.
Encoding bitmap images

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: A bitmap image is a grid of pixels. Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary code, and the codes are stored in order, row by row. The number of bits per pixel is the colour depth: 1 bit gives 2 colours (black and white), 8 bits give 256 colours and 24 bits give over 16.7 million colours (8 bits each for red, green and blue). A file header at the start of the file records information the software needs to rebuild the image, such as the file type, image width and height, and colour depth.

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: Image resolution is a property of the image (how many pixels it contains); screen resolution is a property of the display.

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: If the image resolution is higher than the screen resolution, the image is scaled down or only part of it is shown.

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text: Enlarging a bitmap beyond its resolution makes the individual pixels visible (pixelation).

fragments.label: Encoding bitmap images
fragments.text:
Colour depth 4 bits → 2^4 = 16 colours
Colour depth 8 bits → 2^8 = 256 colours
Colour depth 24 bits → 2^24 = 16,777,216 colours
Calculating bitmap file size

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: The pixel data in a bitmap take up (number of pixels) × (colour depth) bits. Multiply the width by the height to find the number of pixels, multiply by the colour depth, then divide by 8 to convert bits to bytes. The result is an estimate, because the file header adds a small amount of extra data.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: Divide by 8 for bytes, then by 1024 for KiB or by 1000 for kB, depending on the unit the question asks for.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: Keep the calculation in one line of working so method marks can be awarded.

fragments.label: Calculating bitmap file size
fragments.text: State that the file header makes the real file slightly larger than the estimate.
Effect of changing resolution and colour depth

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: Increasing the image resolution gives more pixels, so finer detail can be shown and the image can be enlarged further before pixelation appears. Increasing the colour depth allows more colours, so shades and gradients look more realistic with less colour banding. Both changes increase the file size in direct proportion: doubling the colour depth doubles the size, and doubling both the width and the height quadruples it.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: Reducing resolution or colour depth reduces file size but lowers quality; this is a trade-off, not a free saving.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: A larger file takes longer to download or transmit and uses more storage.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text: Always link a change to both effects the question asks for: quality and file size.

fragments.label: Effect of changing resolution and colour depth
fragments.text:
An image is 2 MiB. Its width and height are both halved and its colour depth is changed from 24 bits to 8 bits.
Pixels fall to ½ × ½ = ¼ of the original
Bits per pixel fall to 8 ÷ 24 = ⅓ of the original
New size = 2 MiB × ¼ × ⅓ ≈ 0.17 MiB
Encoding vector graphics

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: A vector graphic does not store pixels. Instead it stores a drawing list: a set of commands describing each drawing object and its properties, such as a circle's centre coordinates, radius, line colour, line width and fill colour. When the image is displayed, the software recalculates every object from these properties, so the graphic can be scaled to any size without losing quality.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: File size depends on the number and complexity of objects, not on the display size.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: Scaling only changes property values, so edges stay sharp at any size.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text: Vector graphics are poor at representing photographs, because natural scenes cannot be broken down into simple shapes.

fragments.label: Encoding vector graphics
fragments.text:
Circle: centre (120, 80), radius 40, line colour black, line width 2, fill colour red
Rectangle: top-left (20, 20), width 60, height 30, line colour blue, fill none
Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Choose a bitmap when the image has continuous tones and fine, irregular detail, such as a photograph or a scanned document. Choose a vector graphic when the image is built from lines and shapes and must be resized, such as a logo, a diagram, a map, a font or a technical drawing. In a justification, name the feature of the task and link it to a property of the format.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Logo printed on a pen and on a billboard → vector, because it must scale without pixelation.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Photograph from a digital camera → bitmap, because each pixel's colour can be captured individually.

fragments.label: Choosing a bitmap or a vector graphic
fragments.text: Simple diagrams are often smaller as vectors; complex photographs would need a vast drawing list.
Sampling sound

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: Sound is an analogue wave: its amplitude varies continuously over time. To store it digitally, the amplitude is measured (sampled) at regular time intervals, and each measurement is rounded to the nearest level that can be stored with the sampling resolution. These binary sample values are stored in order, with a file header recording details such as the sampling rate and sampling resolution. Played back, the samples are converted into an approximation of the original wave.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: Analogue data vary continuously; digital data take discrete values.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: The sampling rate controls how often the wave is measured; the sampling resolution controls how precisely each measurement is stored.

fragments.label: Sampling sound
fragments.text: A sampling resolution of n bits gives 2^n possible amplitude levels, e.g. 16 bits gives 65,536.
Sound quality and file size

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: A higher sampling rate captures changes in the wave more often, so rapid changes (higher frequencies) are represented and the playback is closer to the original. A higher sampling resolution rounds each sample less, so the amplitude is recorded more accurately with less quantisation error. Both improve accuracy but increase the file size: file size = sampling rate × sampling resolution × duration in seconds (× number of channels).

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: Doubling the sampling rate or the sampling resolution doubles the file size.

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: Stereo sound has two channels, so it needs twice the data of mono.

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text: Beyond a certain point, extra quality cannot be heard, so a larger file brings no practical benefit.

fragments.label: Sound quality and file size
fragments.text:
Sampling rate = 44,100 Hz, sampling resolution = 16 bits, 2 channels, 30 seconds
Bits = 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 30 = 42,336,000 bits
Bytes = 42,336,000 ÷ 8 = 5,292,000 bytes
MiB = 5,292,000 ÷ 1024 ÷ 1024 ≈ 5.05 MiB
What is colour depth?

fragments.label: What is colour depth?
fragments.text: The number of bits used to represent the colour of each pixel.
How many colours can a 12-bit colour depth represent?

fragments.label: How many colours can a 12-bit colour depth represent?
fragments.text: 2^12 = 4096 colours.
How do you estimate the file size of a bitmap?

fragments.label: How do you estimate the file size of a bitmap?
fragments.text: Width × height × colour depth gives bits; divide by 8 for bytes.
What does a vector graphic's drawing list contain?

fragments.label: What does a vector graphic's drawing list contain?
fragments.text: Commands defining each drawing object and its properties, such as coordinates, size and colours.
Why does a vector graphic not pixelate when enlarged?

fragments.label: Why does a vector graphic not pixelate when enlarged?
fragments.text: Each object is recalculated from its properties at the new size rather than stretching stored pixels.
What is the difference between sampling rate and sampling resolution?

fragments.label: What is the difference between sampling rate and sampling resolution?
fragments.text: Sampling rate is how many samples are taken per second; sampling resolution is how many bits store each sample.
What is the formula for the size of a sound file?

fragments.label: What is the formula for the size of a sound file?
fragments.text: Sampling rate × sampling resolution × duration in seconds × number of channels (in bits).
What does a file header store?

fragments.label: What does a file header store?
fragments.text: Information about the file needed to decode it, such as file type, dimensions and colour depth, or sampling rate and resolution.

Compression reduces the size of a file so it takes less storage and transmits faster. Paper 1 asks why compression is needed, what separates lossy from lossless methods, which method suits a given file and use, and how different file types are compressed, with run-length encoding (RLE) as the method you must be able to apply and trace.

fragments.label: Compression
fragments.text: Encoding data so that it uses fewer bits than the original representation.

fragments.label: Lossless compression
fragments.text: Compression in which no data are lost, so the original file can be reconstructed exactly.

fragments.label: Lossy compression
fragments.text: Compression that permanently removes data judged to be unnecessary, so the original cannot be reconstructed exactly.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: A lossless method that replaces a run of identical consecutive values with a single copy of the value and a count of how many times it repeats.

fragments.label: Dictionary (token) compression
fragments.text: A lossless method that replaces repeated words or patterns with short codes stored in a dictionary.

fragments.label: Perceptual coding
fragments.text: A lossy technique that removes the parts of a sound or image that human senses are least able to notice.

fragments.label: Compression ratio
fragments.text: Original size divided by compressed size; a higher ratio means greater compression.
Why compression is needed

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Uncompressed images, audio and video are very large. Compressing them means less storage space is used, files transfer and download faster, less bandwidth is used on a network, and media can be streamed in real time without long buffering. Compression is used for email attachments, web pages, streaming services, backups and archives.

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Smaller files → faster transmission → lower data costs and less network congestion.

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Compression and decompression take processing time, which is the price paid for smaller files.

fragments.label: Why compression is needed
fragments.text: Both sender and receiver need compatible software to compress and decompress.
Lossless and lossy compression

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Lossless compression finds patterns or redundancy in the data and records them more efficiently; decompressing gives back every original bit. Lossy compression goes further by discarding data, usually detail that people will barely notice, so it achieves much smaller files, but the removed data are lost permanently and quality falls with each extra level of compression.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Lossless is essential for text, program files, spreadsheets and databases, where one changed bit could corrupt meaning or stop a program working.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Lossy suits photographs, music and video for streaming or the web, where a small loss of quality is acceptable for a large saving.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text: Once lossy compression has been applied, the discarded data cannot be recovered by decompressing.

fragments.label: Lossless and lossy compression
fragments.text:
A program's executable file must be sent to users → lossless, because any lost bit would change the instructions and the program might not run.
A holiday photo is uploaded to social media → lossy, because the file becomes much smaller and the loss of fine detail is not noticeable on a phone screen.
Run-length encoding (RLE)

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: RLE replaces each run of repeated consecutive values with a count and one copy of the value. It works well on data with long runs, such as simple graphics with large areas of one colour, but can make data with few repeats larger, because every single value now needs a count as well.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: RLE is lossless: expanding each count/value pair gives back the exact original.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: In a bitmap, each row of pixels is encoded as runs of colour codes.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text: In text, a flag character is often used to mark where an encoded run starts, so single characters can be left unencoded.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text:
Original: AAAAABBBCCCCCCCCD (17 characters)
Runs: 5 × A, 3 × B, 8 × C, 1 × D
Encoded: 5A 3B 8C 1D (8 characters)
The data have been reduced from 17 to 8 characters.

fragments.label: Run-length encoding (RLE)
fragments.text:
Original: ABCDEF (6 characters)
Encoded: 1A 1B 1C 1D 1E 1F (12 characters)
With no repeated runs, RLE doubles the size, which is why it only suits data with long runs.
Compressing text files

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: Text must always be compressed losslessly. A common approach is dictionary-based: repeated words or groups of characters are stored once in a dictionary, and each occurrence in the file is replaced by a short index into the dictionary. RLE can also be used where characters repeat consecutively, such as runs of spaces.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: The dictionary must be stored with or be known to the decompressor, which adds a small overhead.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text: The more often a word repeats, the greater the saving.

fragments.label: Compressing text files
fragments.text:
Dictionary: 1 = 'the', 2 = 'cat', 3 = 'sat'
'the cat sat the cat' → 1 2 3 1 2
Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: A bitmap can be compressed losslessly with RLE, which is effective on images with large areas of the same colour. Lossy methods reduce the colour depth, reduce the resolution, or group together pixels of similar colour and store them as one colour, which works well on photographs where neighbouring pixels are similar. A vector graphic is already compact because it stores a drawing list, but its text-based drawing list can be further compressed losslessly, for example with dictionary methods.

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: Reducing colour depth or resolution before saving is a form of lossy compression.

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: Lossy image compression can create visible artefacts such as blockiness or colour banding at high compression levels.

fragments.label: Compressing bitmap images and vector graphics
fragments.text: Vector graphics should use lossless compression so that object properties are not altered.
Compressing sound files

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Lossy sound compression uses perceptual coding: it removes sounds outside the range of human hearing, and quieter sounds that are masked by louder sounds at the same time. The sampling rate or sampling resolution can also be reduced. Lossless audio compression exists for situations where perfect quality is needed, such as studio master recordings, but it gives much smaller savings.

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Removing frequencies humans cannot hear reduces size with no audible loss.

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Reducing the sampling rate or resolution lowers accuracy, so quality falls noticeably at extreme settings.

fragments.label: Compressing sound files
fragments.text: Streaming services use lossy compression so music plays without buffering on limited bandwidth.
Give two reasons for compressing files.

fragments.label: Give two reasons for compressing files.
fragments.text: Any two of: less storage space, faster transmission or download, less bandwidth used, allows real-time streaming.
What is the key difference between lossless and lossy compression?

fragments.label: What is the key difference between lossless and lossy compression?
fragments.text: Lossless allows the original to be reconstructed exactly; lossy permanently removes data.
Encode WWWWWBBBWW using RLE.

fragments.label: Encode WWWWWBBBWW using RLE.
fragments.text: 5W 3B 2W.
Why must text files use lossless compression?

fragments.label: Why must text files use lossless compression?
fragments.text: Losing any character would change the content and meaning of the text.
What is perceptual coding?

fragments.label: What is perceptual coding?
fragments.text: Lossy sound compression that removes sounds humans cannot hear or would not notice, such as quiet sounds masked by louder ones.
When does RLE work badly?

fragments.label: When does RLE work badly?
fragments.text: When the data contain few consecutive repeated values, because each value needs a count too and the file may grow.
How can a bitmap be compressed with a lossy method?

fragments.label: How can a bitmap be compressed with a lossy method?
fragments.text: Reduce the resolution or colour depth, or group similar colours together and store them as one colour.

This is one of the broadest AS topics. Paper 1 asks you to compare LANs and WANs, client-server and peer-to-peer models, and network topologies; describe the hardware that builds a LAN and connects it to the internet; explain Ethernet and CSMA/CD, cloud computing and bit streaming; and explain how IP addresses, URLs and DNS let data find its way across the internet. Most marks come from precise definitions and justified choices for a given scenario.

fragments.label: Local area network (LAN)
fragments.text: A network of connected devices over a small geographical area, such as a single building or site, usually owned by one organisation.

fragments.label: Wide area network (WAN)
fragments.text: A network covering a large geographical area, often linking LANs, using communication infrastructure owned by third parties.

fragments.label: Client-server model
fragments.text: A network model in which central servers provide services and resources that client devices request.

fragments.label: Peer-to-peer model
fragments.text: A network model with no central server, in which each device can both share and request resources.

fragments.label: Topology
fragments.text: The physical or logical arrangement of the devices and connections in a network.

fragments.label: Router
fragments.text: A device that forwards packets between different networks, choosing a route using the destination IP address.

fragments.label: Switch
fragments.text: A device that connects devices within a LAN and forwards each frame only to the device whose MAC address matches the destination.

fragments.label: CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection: the Ethernet method for sharing a medium, detecting collisions and retransmitting after a random delay.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: Transmitting a continuous sequence of bits, such as audio or video, which is played as it arrives rather than after the whole file has downloaded.

fragments.label: IP address
fragments.text: A numerical address that identifies a device on a network so that packets can be routed to it.

fragments.label: Domain Name Service (DNS)
fragments.text: A distributed system of servers that translates domain names into IP addresses.

fragments.label: Cloud computing
fragments.text: Using storage, processing or software provided over the internet by remote servers instead of local hardware.
Why networks are used; LANs and WANs

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: Networking devices lets users share resources such as printers, files, storage and an internet connection, communicate by email and messaging, and be managed centrally (software updates, backups and security settings applied from one place). A LAN covers a small area such as a school or office, with infrastructure owned by the organisation, and typically gives high data transfer rates. A WAN covers a large area, such as a country or the whole world, usually by connecting LANs through leased lines, the telephone network or satellites owned by telecommunications companies. The internet is the largest WAN.

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: LAN: small area, organisation-owned hardware, higher speeds, fewer errors.

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: WAN: large area, third-party infrastructure, generally lower speeds and higher latency.

fragments.label: Why networks are used; LANs and WANs
fragments.text: Benefit of a network always links to a resource being shared or a task being centralised.
Client-server and peer-to-peer models

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: In the client-server model, clients send requests and dedicated servers respond, for example a file server, print server, email server or web server. Data and security are managed centrally, so backups and access rights are easier to control, but the servers are costly and are a single point of failure unless duplicated. In a peer-to-peer network every device (peer) has equal status and shares its own resources directly with others. It is cheap and simple for a few devices, but files are spread across machines, backups are harder, and security depends on each user.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: A thin client relies heavily on the server for processing and storage; it needs a constant connection but is cheap and easy to manage.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: A thick (fat) client does most of its processing and storage locally; it can keep working if the server is unavailable but needs more powerful hardware.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text: Justify client-server for large organisations needing central security and backup; justify peer-to-peer for small homes or offices, or for sharing files among many users without a central bottleneck.

fragments.label: Client-server and peer-to-peer models
fragments.text:
A school with 800 students: client-server, because accounts, permissions and backups must be controlled centrally and students must be able to log in from any computer.
Three friends sharing files at home: peer-to-peer, because a dedicated server would be an unnecessary cost for so few devices.
Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: In a bus topology all devices share one backbone cable with a terminator at each end; every packet travels along the whole cable and each device checks whether it is the destination. It is cheap, but a break in the backbone stops the whole network, and performance falls as traffic grows because of collisions. In a star topology each device has its own link to a central switch, which forwards each packet only to the destination device, so one broken link affects only one device, but the central switch is a single point of failure. In a mesh topology devices are connected to several others, so packets can take alternative routes; a full mesh is very reliable but needs a lot of cabling. A hybrid topology combines two or more topologies, such as several stars joined by a bus.

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: Star is the most common LAN topology: easy to add devices and fewer collisions.

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: Mesh is used where reliability matters, and the internet itself is a partial mesh of routers.

fragments.label: Bus, star, mesh and hybrid topologies
fragments.text: Wireless networks are often described as a mesh or star around a wireless access point.
Cloud computing

fragments.label: Cloud computing
fragments.text: Cloud computing provides storage, processing power or software over the internet from a provider's servers. A public cloud is owned by a provider and shared by many customers who pay for what they use. A private cloud is used by one organisation only, either on its own premises or hosted for it, giving more control over security at higher cost.

fragments.label: Cloud computing
fragments.text: Benefits: no need to buy and maintain servers, storage can be scaled up or down quickly, data can be accessed from anywhere, and the provider handles backups and updates.

fragments.label: Cloud computing
fragments.text: Drawbacks: needs a reliable internet connection, ongoing subscription costs, less control over where data are stored, and security and privacy depend on a third party.

fragments.label: Cloud computing
fragments.text: Data protection laws may restrict storing personal data on servers in another country.
Wired and wireless networks

fragments.label: Wired and wireless networks
fragments.text: Wired networks use copper cable (twisted pair or coaxial) or fibre-optic cable. Fibre carries light, so it has the highest bandwidth, works over long distances and does not suffer electrical interference, but it is expensive. Wireless networks use radio waves (Wi-Fi), microwaves or satellites. They let users move around and avoid cabling costs, but they are slower, have a limited range, suffer interference from walls and other devices, and are easier to intercept, so encryption is essential.

fragments.label: Wired and wireless networks
fragments.text: Wired: faster, more reliable and more secure; less flexible and costly to install in existing buildings.

fragments.label: Wired and wireless networks
fragments.text: Wireless: flexible and cheap to extend; lower speed, interference and security risks.

fragments.label: Wired and wireless networks
fragments.text: Satellites cover remote areas but add significant delay because of the distance the signal travels.
LAN hardware and routers

fragments.label: LAN hardware and routers
fragments.text: Each device needs a network interface card (NIC), or a wireless NIC (WNIC), which has a unique MAC address and connects the device to the medium. A switch connects devices in a star LAN and forwards frames only to the intended device using MAC addresses. A wireless access point (WAP) lets wireless devices join the wired LAN. A server provides shared services. A repeater boosts a weakened signal so it can travel further, and a bridge joins two LAN segments that use the same protocol so they act as one network. A router connects different networks, such as a LAN to the internet: it reads the destination IP address of each packet and uses its routing table to forward it towards its destination by the best available route.

fragments.label: LAN hardware and routers
fragments.text: A switch works within one network using MAC addresses; a router works between networks using IP addresses.

fragments.label: LAN hardware and routers
fragments.text: A home 'router' usually combines a router, switch, WAP and modem in one box.

fragments.label: LAN hardware and routers
fragments.text: A router can also assign private IP addresses to local devices and translate them to the network's public address.
Ethernet and CSMA/CD

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Ethernet is the standard protocol family for wired LANs. Data are sent in frames that contain the source and destination MAC addresses. Where devices share a medium, two devices may transmit at the same moment and their signals collide. CSMA/CD manages this: a device listens to check the medium is idle before sending (carrier sense); if a collision is detected while transmitting, it stops, sends a jam signal so all devices know, waits a random time, then tries again. Because each device waits a different random time, a repeat collision is unlikely.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: The random back-off is the key point: fixed waits would cause the same collision again.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: After repeated collisions the maximum random wait increases.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text: Modern switched Ethernet gives each device its own link to the switch, so collisions rarely occur.

fragments.label: Ethernet and CSMA/CD
fragments.text:
1. Device checks whether the medium is idle
2. If busy, it waits; if idle, it starts transmitting
3. It keeps monitoring the medium while transmitting
4. A collision is detected, so it stops and sends a jam signal
5. It waits a random back-off time
6. It returns to step 1 and retransmits
Bit streaming

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: In bit streaming, audio or video is sent as a continuous stream of bits and played as it arrives. The data are compressed, and a buffer on the receiving device stores a few seconds ahead so playback continues smoothly if the connection briefly slows. On-demand streaming sends pre-recorded content (such as a film) whenever a user chooses to watch it, so it can be paused, rewound and fast-forwarded. Real-time (live) streaming sends an event as it happens, such as a live sports match, so the viewer cannot skip ahead.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: The bit rate is the number of bits per second the stream needs; higher quality means a higher bit rate.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: If the broadband speed is lower than the stream's bit rate, the buffer empties and playback stops to rebuffer.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text: Services often lower the resolution automatically when the connection is slow.

fragments.label: Bit streaming
fragments.text:
A 1080p stream needs 5 Mbps. The household has 20 Mbps and two people stream at once.
Required = 2 × 5 = 10 Mbps, which is below 20 Mbps, so both streams should play smoothly, with capacity left for other traffic.
The internet, the WWW and internet hardware

fragments.label: The internet, the WWW and internet hardware
fragments.text: The internet is the global network of interconnected networks: the physical infrastructure of devices, routers and links. The World Wide Web is a service that runs on the internet: a collection of linked web pages and resources accessed using HTTP or HTTPS through a browser. Email and file transfer are other services that also use the internet. Hardware supporting the internet includes modems, which convert between the digital signals of a computer and the analogue signals of a telephone line; the public switched telephone network (PSTN); dedicated (leased) lines rented for exclusive use by one organisation; and the cell phone network, which uses radio masts and base stations to give mobile devices internet access.

fragments.label: The internet, the WWW and internet hardware
fragments.text: Internet = the network (hardware); WWW = one service using it (web pages).

fragments.label: The internet, the WWW and internet hardware
fragments.text: A dedicated line gives a guaranteed, secure, constant connection, but is expensive.

fragments.label: The internet, the WWW and internet hardware
fragments.text: Cellular networks provide mobile access; each cell has a base station connected to the wider network.
IP addresses and subnetting

fragments.label: IP addresses and subnetting
fragments.text: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four denary numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, for example 192.168.10.25. This allows about 4.3 billion addresses, which is not enough for every device. IPv6 uses 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, giving a vastly larger address space. A public IP address is unique on the internet and can be reached from outside; private addresses (such as the 192.168.x.x range) are used inside a LAN, can be reused by other LANs, and reach the internet through the router's public address. A static IP address stays the same and is used for servers that must always be found at the same address; a dynamic address is assigned automatically each time a device connects.

fragments.label: IP addresses and subnetting
fragments.text: Subnetting splits a network into smaller sub-networks: part of the address identifies the network (and subnet) and the rest identifies the host.

fragments.label: IP addresses and subnetting
fragments.text: Subnetting improves security and performance by keeping traffic within a department and reducing broadcast traffic.

fragments.label: IP addresses and subnetting
fragments.text: IPv6 groups of leading zeros can be shortened, and one run of all-zero groups can be replaced by ::.

fragments.label: IP addresses and subnetting
fragments.text:
192.168.300.4 → invalid: 300 is greater than 255, so it does not fit in 8 bits.
10.0.0.256 → invalid for the same reason.
172.16.5.1 → valid: four numbers, each 0–255.
URLs and the Domain Name Service

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) gives the location of a resource on the web, for example https://www.example.com/notes/index.html. It is made of the protocol (https), the domain name (www.example.com) and the path to the file (/notes/index.html). Computers route by IP address, so the domain name must be looked up. The browser asks a DNS server for the IP address. If that server does not have the entry, it asks other DNS servers in a hierarchy until the address is found. The IP address is returned to the browser, which then sends its request to the web server at that address.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: Domain names are easier for people to remember than IP addresses.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: DNS results are cached so repeat lookups are faster.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text: If a website's server moves to a new IP address, only the DNS record needs updating, not the URL.

fragments.label: URLs and the Domain Name Service
fragments.text:
1. The user types a URL into the browser
2. The browser extracts the domain name and sends it to a DNS server
3. The DNS server looks up the IP address, querying other DNS servers if necessary
4. The IP address is returned to the browser
5. The browser sends an HTTP(S) request to that IP address
6. The web server returns the page, which the browser renders
Give two differences between a LAN and a WAN.

fragments.label: Give two differences between a LAN and a WAN.
fragments.text: A LAN covers a small area and uses the organisation's own hardware; a WAN covers a large area and uses third-party infrastructure such as leased lines.
What is the difference between a thin client and a thick client?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a thin client and a thick client?
fragments.text: A thin client relies on the server for most processing and storage; a thick client processes and stores data locally.
What does a router do?

fragments.label: What does a router do?
fragments.text: It forwards packets between networks, using the destination IP address and a routing table to choose the route.
What happens in CSMA/CD when a collision is detected?

fragments.label: What happens in CSMA/CD when a collision is detected?
fragments.text: Transmission stops, a jam signal is sent, the device waits a random time and then retransmits.
What is the difference between on-demand and real-time streaming?

fragments.label: What is the difference between on-demand and real-time streaming?
fragments.text: On-demand streams pre-recorded content when requested and can be paused or skipped; real-time streams a live event as it happens.
How many bits are in IPv4 and IPv6 addresses?

fragments.label: How many bits are in IPv4 and IPv6 addresses?
fragments.text: IPv4 is 32 bits; IPv6 is 128 bits.
Why is a static IP address used for a web server?

fragments.label: Why is a static IP address used for a web server?
fragments.text: So its address never changes and DNS records keep pointing to it.
What is the role of DNS?

fragments.label: What is the role of DNS?
fragments.text: It translates a domain name into the IP address of the server hosting the resource.

A computer system needs input, output, primary memory and secondary storage, and Paper 1 expects you to explain why each is needed and how common devices work internally. Questions ask you to describe the operation of printers, disks, flash memory, touchscreens and other devices step by step, compare types of RAM and ROM, explain buffers and embedded systems, and describe how monitoring and control systems use sensors, actuators and feedback.

fragments.label: Primary memory
fragments.text: Memory directly accessible by the processor (RAM and ROM), holding the data and instructions currently in use.

fragments.label: Secondary storage
fragments.text: Non-volatile storage, such as a hard disk or SSD, that keeps programs and data permanently when the power is off.

fragments.label: Volatile
fragments.text: Describes memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off.

fragments.label: Embedded system
fragments.text: A computer system with a dedicated function built into a larger device, such as a washing machine controller.

fragments.label: Buffer
fragments.text: An area of memory that temporarily holds data being transferred between devices or processes that work at different speeds.

fragments.label: Sensor
fragments.text: An input device that measures a physical quantity, such as temperature or light, and sends the reading to a computer.

fragments.label: Actuator
fragments.text: An output device, such as a motor, valve or heater, that performs a physical action when signalled by a computer.

fragments.label: Feedback
fragments.text: Using the output of a control system to affect its next input, so the system can keep a variable close to a set value.
Input, output, memory and storage

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: Input devices capture data and instructions from users or the environment so the computer has something to process. Output devices present the results in a form people or other devices can use. Primary memory holds the programs and data currently being used, so the processor can access them quickly. Because RAM is volatile, secondary storage is needed to keep programs and files permanently. Removable storage, such as USB flash drives and optical discs, lets data be carried between computers and kept as off-site backups.

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: The processor can only execute programs that are in primary memory; they are loaded there from secondary storage.

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: Secondary storage is slower than RAM but cheaper per gigabyte and much larger.

fragments.label: Input, output, memory and storage
fragments.text: Link each component to its purpose in the scenario given, not just its name.
Embedded systems

fragments.label: Embedded systems
fragments.text: An embedded system is a microprocessor or microcontroller with its own memory and input/output, built into a larger device to carry out one dedicated task. Examples include the controllers in washing machines, microwave ovens, car engine management systems, traffic lights and fitness trackers. The program is usually stored in ROM or flash memory and runs as soon as the device is switched on.

fragments.label: Embedded systems
fragments.text: Benefits: small, cheap to mass-produce, low power use, reliable because the task is fixed, and quick to respond.

fragments.label: Embedded systems
fragments.text: Drawbacks: difficult or impossible to upgrade, hard to repair, and a device connected to the internet may be vulnerable to hacking if it cannot be updated.

fragments.label: Embedded systems
fragments.text: A general-purpose computer can run many programs; an embedded system is designed for one.
Laser printers and 3D printers

fragments.label: Laser printers and 3D printers
fragments.text: In a laser printer, the printing drum is given a positive electrostatic charge. A laser beam, directed by a rotating mirror, removes the charge from areas of the drum that match the image. The drum is coated with positively charged toner, which sticks only to the discharged areas. Negatively charged paper passes over the drum and attracts the toner, then the paper passes through a fuser, where heated rollers melt the toner onto it. Finally the charge is removed from the drum ready for the next page. A 3D printer builds a solid object layer by layer from a digital design: the design is sliced into thin layers, and material such as plastic filament is heated and extruded through a nozzle (or resin is hardened by light) to form each layer on top of the previous one.

fragments.label: Laser printers and 3D printers
fragments.text: Laser printers are fast and suited to high-volume text printing; the whole page is prepared on the drum before printing.

fragments.label: Laser printers and 3D printers
fragments.text: 3D printing is used for prototypes, custom medical implants and spare parts.

fragments.label: Laser printers and 3D printers
fragments.text: Give laser printer steps in the correct order: charge, laser discharges image, toner, paper, fuser, discharge drum.
Microphones and speakers

fragments.label: Microphones and speakers
fragments.text: In a microphone, sound waves make a diaphragm vibrate. The diaphragm is attached to a coil of wire around a magnet, so its movement induces a varying electrical current that matches the sound wave. This analogue signal is converted to digital by an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC). A speaker works in reverse: digital data are converted to an analogue signal by a digital-to-analogue converter (DAC) and amplified. The varying current passes through a coil attached to a cone, producing a changing magnetic field that pushes against a permanent magnet, so the cone vibrates and creates sound waves.

fragments.label: Microphones and speakers
fragments.text: Microphone: sound → vibration → electrical signal → ADC.

fragments.label: Microphones and speakers
fragments.text: Speaker: DAC → amplified signal → coil and magnet → cone vibrates → sound.

fragments.label: Microphones and speakers
fragments.text: The frequency of the vibration sets the pitch; the amplitude sets the volume.
Magnetic, solid state and optical storage

fragments.label: Magnetic, solid state and optical storage
fragments.text: A magnetic hard disk has platters coated with magnetic material that spin at high speed. Read/write heads on an actuator arm move across the surface; to write, a head magnetises tiny areas in one of two directions to represent 0 or 1, and to read, it detects the direction of magnetisation. Data are arranged in concentric tracks divided into sectors. Solid state (flash) memory has no moving parts: data are stored as electric charge trapped in floating-gate transistors arranged in a grid of NAND or NOR cells, and blocks are erased electrically before being rewritten. An optical disc reader shines a laser onto the spinning disc; the surface has pits and lands along a spiral track, and the change between them alters the reflected light, which a sensor reads as binary. An optical writer uses a stronger laser to change the reflectivity of a dye or alloy layer to create the equivalent of pits.

fragments.label: Magnetic, solid state and optical storage
fragments.text: SSDs are faster, quieter, lighter, more robust and use less power than hard disks, but cost more per gigabyte and have a limited number of write cycles.

fragments.label: Magnetic, solid state and optical storage
fragments.text: Hard disks give large capacity cheaply, but moving parts make them slower and vulnerable to shocks.

fragments.label: Magnetic, solid state and optical storage
fragments.text: Optical discs are cheap and portable but have low capacity and slow access compared with other storage.
Touchscreens and virtual reality headsets

fragments.label: Touchscreens and virtual reality headsets
fragments.text: A capacitive touchscreen has a layer that stores electric charge. A finger conducts electricity, so touching the screen changes the charge at that point; sensors at the corners or in a grid measure the change, and the processor calculates the location. Capacitive screens support multi-touch but do not work with an ordinary gloved finger. A resistive touchscreen has two flexible conductive layers separated by a small gap; pressing brings the layers into contact, completing a circuit, and the position is calculated from the change in voltage. A virtual reality headset has a separate display (or half of a screen) for each eye, showing slightly different images to create a 3D effect, with lenses to focus the image. Sensors such as gyroscopes and accelerometers track head movement, so the image is updated to match where the user is looking.

fragments.label: Touchscreens and virtual reality headsets
fragments.text: Capacitive: clear, durable, multi-touch; needs a conductive touch.

fragments.label: Touchscreens and virtual reality headsets
fragments.text: Resistive: cheap, works with a stylus or gloves; less clear and more easily damaged.

fragments.label: Touchscreens and virtual reality headsets
fragments.text: VR headsets need a high refresh rate and fast tracking to avoid motion sickness.
Buffers

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: A buffer is a temporary area of memory used when data move between two devices or processes that work at different speeds. For example, the processor can send a document to a printer's buffer much faster than the printer can print it, and then continue with other work while the printer empties the buffer. In video streaming, incoming data fill a buffer so playback can continue smoothly if the network briefly slows.

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: A buffer lets the faster device carry on with other tasks instead of waiting.

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: When a printer buffer is empty, the printer sends an interrupt to request more data.

fragments.label: Buffers
fragments.text: A keyboard buffer holds keypresses until the program is ready to read them.
RAM and ROM

fragments.label: RAM and ROM
fragments.text: RAM (random access memory) is volatile read/write memory that holds the operating system, programs and data currently in use. ROM (read-only memory) is non-volatile and holds data that must not be lost or changed, such as the start-up instructions (bootstrap) that run when the computer is switched on. Dynamic RAM (DRAM) stores each bit as charge in a capacitor, which leaks, so it must be refreshed thousands of times a second. Static RAM (SRAM) stores each bit in a flip-flop circuit that does not need refreshing. SRAM is faster but more expensive and takes more space per bit, so it is used for cache memory; DRAM is cheaper and denser, so it is used for main memory.

fragments.label: RAM and ROM
fragments.text: PROM: programmed once after manufacture; the contents cannot then be changed.

fragments.label: RAM and ROM
fragments.text: EPROM: can be erased by exposing the chip to ultraviolet light and then reprogrammed; the chip is usually removed to do this.

fragments.label: RAM and ROM
fragments.text: EEPROM: can be erased and rewritten electrically while in the circuit, a byte or block at a time; flash memory is a type of EEPROM.

fragments.label: RAM and ROM
fragments.text: Firmware updates in modern devices are possible because the firmware is stored in EEPROM or flash.
Monitoring and control systems

fragments.label: Monitoring and control systems
fragments.text: A monitoring system uses sensors to take readings at regular intervals, stores and processes them, and may output warnings or graphs, but it does not change the environment. Examples include hospital patient monitoring and weather stations. A control system also takes sensor readings, but compares them with a stored set value and uses actuators to change conditions. Sensor readings are analogue, so an ADC converts them to digital; signals to actuators may need a DAC. Feedback makes control continuous: the output affects the next sensor reading, so the system keeps adjusting to hold the value close to the set point.

fragments.label: Monitoring and control systems
fragments.text: Monitoring = read and report; control = read, compare, act.

fragments.label: Monitoring and control systems
fragments.text: Typical sensors: temperature, light, pressure, moisture, infrared (motion), pH, gas.

fragments.label: Monitoring and control systems
fragments.text: The computer does not measure anything itself; the sensor measures and the computer processes.

fragments.label: Monitoring and control systems
fragments.text: Describe control as a loop: read, convert, compare, act, repeat.

fragments.label: Monitoring and control systems
fragments.text:
1. A temperature sensor measures the air temperature
2. An ADC converts the analogue reading to digital
3. The microprocessor compares the reading with the stored set value (e.g. 24 °C)
4. If it is too low, a signal switches the heater on; if too high, a signal opens the window using an actuator
5. The new temperature affects the next reading (feedback)
6. The process repeats continuously
Why is secondary storage needed?

fragments.label: Why is secondary storage needed?
fragments.text: RAM is volatile, so programs and data must be kept permanently on non-volatile storage when the power is off.
Give one benefit and one drawback of embedded systems.

fragments.label: Give one benefit and one drawback of embedded systems.
fragments.text: Benefit: small, cheap, low power or reliable. Drawback: hard to upgrade or repair, or vulnerable if connected and not updated.
What is the purpose of the fuser in a laser printer?

fragments.label: What is the purpose of the fuser in a laser printer?
fragments.text: Heated rollers melt the toner so it bonds permanently to the paper.
Why does DRAM need refreshing?

fragments.label: Why does DRAM need refreshing?
fragments.text: Each bit is stored as charge in a capacitor, which leaks away over time.
How is an EEPROM different from an EPROM?

fragments.label: How is an EEPROM different from an EPROM?
fragments.text: EEPROM is erased electrically in the circuit; EPROM is erased with ultraviolet light.
Why is a buffer used when printing?

fragments.label: Why is a buffer used when printing?
fragments.text: The printer is much slower than the processor, so data are held in the buffer and the processor can continue other work.
What is the difference between a sensor and an actuator?

fragments.label: What is the difference between a sensor and an actuator?
fragments.text: A sensor measures a physical quantity as input; an actuator performs a physical action as output.
How does a capacitive touchscreen detect a touch?

fragments.label: How does a capacitive touchscreen detect a touch?
fragments.text: The finger changes the electric charge at the touch point, and sensors measure the change to calculate the position.

Logic gates are the building blocks of every digital circuit. Paper 1 expects you to know the six gates and their truth tables, and to move confidently between four forms of the same logic: a problem statement, a logic expression, a logic circuit and a truth table. Many questions give one form and ask for another, so a systematic method for each conversion is worth more than memorising examples.

fragments.label: Logic gate
fragments.text: An electronic component that performs a Boolean operation on one or more binary inputs to produce a single binary output.

fragments.label: Truth table
fragments.text: A table listing every possible combination of inputs to a gate or circuit and the output produced by each.

fragments.label: Logic expression
fragments.text: A statement of a circuit's output using inputs and the operators AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR, e.g. X = (A AND B) OR NOT C.

fragments.label: Logic circuit
fragments.text: A combination of connected logic gates that produces an output from a set of inputs.

fragments.label: NAND gate
fragments.text: An AND gate followed by NOT: the output is 0 only when all inputs are 1.

fragments.label: NOR gate
fragments.text: An OR gate followed by NOT: the output is 1 only when all inputs are 0.

fragments.label: XOR (EOR) gate
fragments.text: Exclusive OR: the output is 1 when the inputs are different and 0 when they are the same.

fragments.label: Sum of products
fragments.text: A way of writing an expression from a truth table by ORing together one AND term for each row where the output is 1.
The six logic gates

fragments.label: The six logic gates
fragments.text: NOT has one input and inverts it. AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1. NAND and NOR are AND and OR with the output inverted. XOR outputs 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1. Every gate except NOT takes two inputs in 9618 questions.

fragments.label: The six logic gates
fragments.text: Symbols: NOT is a triangle with a small circle at the output; AND has a flat back and a semicircular front; OR has a curved back and a pointed front.

fragments.label: The six logic gates
fragments.text: A small circle (bubble) at the output means 'inverted': NAND is the AND symbol with a bubble, NOR is the OR symbol with a bubble.

fragments.label: The six logic gates
fragments.text: XOR is the OR symbol with an extra curved line across the inputs.

fragments.label: The six logic gates
fragments.text: Useful shortcuts: AND is like multiplication, OR is 'any 1', XOR is 'different'.
From a problem statement to an expression

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text: Read the statement carefully and assign each condition to an input. Look for the connecting words: 'and', 'or', 'not', 'but not' and 'either … or … but not both'. Build the expression in brackets so the order of operations is clear, then check it against the statement with one or two sample inputs.

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text: 'Either A or B but not both' is XOR.

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text: 'Neither A nor B' is NOR (equivalently NOT A AND NOT B).

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text: 'Not both A and B' is NAND.

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text: Use brackets around every sub-expression to avoid ambiguity.

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text:
An alarm (X) sounds if the system is armed (A = 1) and either a door is open (D = 1) or motion is detected (M = 1).
X = A AND (D OR M)

fragments.label: From a problem statement to an expression
fragments.text:
A pump (P) runs if the tank is not full (F = 0) and either the manual switch is on (S = 1) or the timer is on (T = 1), but not when both switch and timer are on.
P = (NOT F) AND (S XOR T)
Building a truth table

fragments.label: Building a truth table
