fragments.text: The methods are not mutually exclusive. A business can assure supplier and process quality, inspect safety-critical output, involve employees through TQM and benchmark delivery reliability.

fragments.label: Choosing and integrating quality approaches
fragments.text: Recommend the sequence as well as the method: contain current failures first, remove causes next, then embed and continuously improve the system.
What makes quality relative rather than absolute?

fragments.label: What makes quality relative rather than absolute?
fragments.text: The required standard depends on fitness for purpose and what the target customer reasonably expects at the promised price and use.
How does quality control differ from quality assurance?

fragments.label: How does quality control differ from quality assurance?
fragments.text: Control detects deviations through inspection or testing; assurance designs standards and checks through the process to prevent defects.
What are the four cost-of-quality categories?

fragments.label: What are the four cost-of-quality categories?
fragments.text: Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure.
What is an internal customer in TQM?

fragments.label: What is an internal customer in TQM?
fragments.text: The employee or process that receives the output of an earlier employee or stage inside the business.
Why can final inspection be expensive even when it protects customers?

fragments.label: Why can final inspection be expensive even when it protects customers?
fragments.text: Resources may already have been wasted, inspectors and tests cost money, and sampling can still miss defects.
What are the final two steps in useful benchmarking?

fragments.label: What are the final two steps in useful benchmarking?
fragments.text: Adapt and implement a suitable practice, then re-measure whether the gap and customer outcome improved.
Why might more prevention cost increase profit?

fragments.label: Why might more prevention cost increase profit?
fragments.text: If it reduces larger failure, rework, warranty and lost-customer costs by more than the additional prevention spend.

Operations strategy builds the process capability needed to deliver a long-term competitive objective. It is not a list of fashionable tools: managers must fit resource constraints, flexibility, technology, ERP, lean methods and project planning to the operation. A strong exam answer traces each choice through capacity, quality, speed, dependability, flexibility and cost, then tests whether finance, people, data and suppliers can make the promised result happen.

fragments.label: Operations strategy
fragments.text: The long-term pattern of decisions about processes, capacity, technology, supply and quality that creates the capabilities required by business strategy.

fragments.label: Process innovation
fragments.text: Introducing a new or materially improved way of producing or delivering a product.

fragments.label: Flexibility
fragments.text: The ability to change output volume, delivery timing or product specification in response to need.

fragments.label: Node / event
fragments.text: A point in an activity-on-arrow network showing when one or more activities start or finish; the event itself consumes no time or resources.

fragments.label: Activity arrow
fragments.text: A task in the project, drawn as an arrow and labelled with its duration; the arrow's direction shows the dependency sequence.

fragments.label: Earliest event time
fragments.text: The earliest time an event can occur after all activities leading into its node have finished.

fragments.label: Latest event time
fragments.text: The latest time an event can occur without delaying completion of the whole project.

fragments.label: ERP
fragments.text: Enterprise Resource Planning: an integrated system that gives functions access to a shared database and coordinated business processes.

fragments.label: Lean production
fragments.text: An approach that seeks greater customer value while removing waste, delay, defects, excess inventory and other non-value-adding activity.

fragments.label: Kaizen
fragments.text: Continuous, usually incremental, improvement involving employees close to the process.

fragments.label: Quality circle
fragments.text: A small group of employees that meets to identify, analyse and propose solutions to work-related quality or process problems.

fragments.label: Simultaneous engineering
fragments.text: Developing linked stages or functions in parallel so that design, production and market requirements influence one another earlier.

fragments.label: Cell production
fragments.text: Organising people and equipment into teams or cells that complete a family of related products or a substantial stage of production.

fragments.label: Critical path
fragments.text: The path of activities with zero total float that determines the project's minimum completion time.

fragments.label: Total float
fragments.text: The maximum time an activity may be delayed without delaying completion of the whole project.

fragments.label: Free float
fragments.text: The maximum time an activity may be delayed without delaying the earliest start of its next activity.

fragments.label: Dummy activity
fragments.text: A zero-time, zero-resource arrow used only to show the correct dependency in an activity-on-arrow network.
Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: An operations proposal is feasible only when the other functions can support it. Marketing determines the demand pattern and the promise made to customers; finance limits investment, working capital and acceptable risk; HR determines whether enough employees have the right skills, contracts and willingness to change. A high-speed automated line may fit a large, stable market but fail when finance is expensive or the product changes frequently.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: Flexibility has three distinct forms. Volume flexibility changes how much is produced; delivery flexibility changes when or how quickly orders are supplied; specification flexibility changes the features or customisation offered. Managers can create flexibility through spare capacity, multi-skilled employees, modular equipment, broad supplier relationships and postponing final customisation. Each creates an opportunity cost: unused capacity, training expense, lower specialisation or more complex coordination.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: The decision rule is strategic fit. A premium made-to-order producer may accept higher unit cost to gain specification and delivery flexibility. A mass producer competing on price may prefer high utilisation and standardisation, provided demand is predictable enough to avoid excess inventory.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: HR constraint: scarce technical skill, resistance, training time, contract flexibility and workforce capacity.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: Marketing constraint: forecast uncertainty, promised lead time, variety, service level and product life cycle.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: Finance constraint: capital budget, borrowing cost, cash tied in inventory and payback risk.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: Evaluate the bottleneck: extra technology is of little value if the binding constraint is people, data or demand.

fragments.label: Start with strategy, resources and the flexibility required
fragments.text: A meal producer wins a retailer contract with volatile weekly volumes. A second fixed line raises maximum capacity but may be idle; cross-training and temporary shifts cost more per unit but protect volume flexibility. The better choice depends on forecast confidence, service penalties, labour availability and the contract duration.
IT, AI and process innovation

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: IT collects, transmits and controls operational information. Examples include computer-aided design, computer-aided manufacture, robotics, barcode or RFID tracking, sensor-based monitoring and automated scheduling. AI can recognise defect patterns, predict equipment failure, estimate demand or adjust schedules. The exam value is in the changed process: faster feedback may reduce downtime, waste and late delivery; consistent machine settings may reduce variation; better forecasts may improve capacity and inventory decisions.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Process innovation may lower variable cost, shorten lead time or enable a different product, but it creates implementation risk. Capital expenditure can raise break-even output and make a fall in demand more damaging. Integration, cybersecurity, data quality, maintenance skill and workforce acceptance affect the realised return. Bias or unusual events can make an AI recommendation unreliable, so managers need validation and human review.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Technology can also reduce flexibility when equipment is dedicated to one design. Compare the whole-life benefit with purchase, installation, migration, training, maintenance, energy, disruption and obsolescence costs—not merely the supplier's claimed labour saving.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: CAD shortens redesign and shares accurate specifications; CAM turns digital designs into consistent machine instructions.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Predictive maintenance uses condition data to intervene before failure, but false alerts or missing data can waste resources.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Automation works best with sufficient volume, stable processes and trained support; human judgement remains important for exceptions.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Pilot, measure a baseline, train users and review outcomes before scaling.

fragments.label: IT, AI and process innovation
fragments.text: Sensors identify rising vibration → maintenance is scheduled before breakdown → fewer unplanned stoppages protect output and delivery reliability → overtime and lost-sales costs may fall. The benefit is conditional on accurate thresholds, available engineers and savings exceeding the system's total cost.
ERP: one data flow across the business

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: ERP links modules such as purchasing, inventory, sales, production, finance and HR to a common database. A confirmed customer order can update the production schedule, material requirement, inventory record, delivery plan, invoice and capacity information. This reduces repeated entry and inconsistent versions of the truth.

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: The operational gain is not simply 'better communication'. Timely inventory data can prevent duplicate orders; product-cost data can improve pricing; an integrated schedule can expose a capacity shortage; sales visibility can speed customer responses; workforce records can support shift planning; and management information can reveal performance by product or location.

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: ERP does not repair a poor process automatically. An organisation may standardise codes, cleanse data, redesign approval routes, train users and phase the launch. Otherwise inaccurate data spread across functions, customisation becomes costly and a failed migration interrupts the whole operation. Central integration also raises cyber and continuity exposure, so access control, backups and tested recovery matter.

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: Benefit conditions: common data definitions, disciplined entry, compatible processes and management support.

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: Risks: high implementation cost, disruption, employee resistance, vendor dependence and loss of poorly planned custom features.

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: Measure outcomes such as stock accuracy, order cycle time, schedule adherence and working capital rather than installation alone.

fragments.label: ERP: one data flow across the business
fragments.text: A manufacturer currently holds separate sales and production spreadsheets. ERP could show a sales-order change immediately to purchasing and scheduling, reducing excess components and late delivery. Yet rushed migration of incorrect bills of materials may make shortages worse, so phased testing and owner accountability for master data are critical.
Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Lean production begins with customer value and process flow. Waste may include defects, overproduction, waiting, unnecessary movement or transport, excess processing, excess inventory and underused employee knowledge. The objective is not cost cutting at any price; it is to remove activity that consumes resources without creating value while protecting quality and resilience.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Kaizen invites frequent small improvements and uses employee knowledge. Quality circles concentrate that participation on defined problems. Cell production can shorten movement, strengthen team ownership and handle product families flexibly, although equipment may be duplicated and teamwork requires training. Simultaneous engineering lets design, production and marketing solve manufacturability or customer problems earlier, reducing late redesign, but parallel work demands strong communication.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: JIT coordinates small, timely deliveries and production with demand. It lowers storage, deterioration and cash tied in inventory and exposes defects quickly. The trade-off is a smaller buffer against supplier failure, transport delay or sudden demand. Supplier quality, information sharing and reliable logistics therefore determine whether a pure JIT system or a selective buffer is more suitable.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Kaizen: low-risk cumulative improvements, but participation can become superficial if suggestions are ignored.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Quality circles: improve problem solving and ownership, but need time, evidence and authority to implement ideas.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Simultaneous engineering: faster launch and earlier cross-functional correction, but coordination errors can spread across parallel work.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Cell production: teamwork, variety and shorter flow, but possible equipment duplication and disruption when one member is absent.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: JIT: lower inventory and faster problem exposure, but greater dependence on stable quality and delivery.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: Waste management: prevent, reduce, reuse or recover waste where the extra resource and environmental benefit exceeds the implementation cost.

fragments.label: Lean tools and the waste they are designed to remove
fragments.text: A furniture maker maps repeated waiting between cutting and finishing. A mixed-skill cell reduces movement, a quality circle redesigns the hand-off and a visual replenishment signal limits work in progress. Output improves only if machinery capacity and finish quality remain balanced; otherwise the bottleneck simply moves.
Implement lean without removing necessary resilience

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: Lean implementation changes behaviour as well as layout. Managers need a measurable problem, process data, employee involvement, supplier coordination and a review cycle. If targets reward output alone, employees may hide defects or produce early, recreating waste. If managers use lean only to remove jobs, trust falls and the knowledge needed for improvement may disappear.

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: A lean operation can retain deliberate resilience. Critical imported components may justify safety stock; a second supplier may cost more but reduce interruption risk; spare maintenance capacity may protect dependability. Evaluation should compare the expected cost of disruption with the cost of the buffer, not assume either maximum stock or zero stock is always efficient.

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: Strategic evaluation integrates the tools. A flexible premium producer may use cells and Kaizen but reject highly dedicated automation. A stable high-volume producer may combine flow automation, ERP scheduling and JIT. The best package depends on demand variation, product variety, supplier power, employee capability, finance and the cost of failure.

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: Use before-and-after measures: lead time, defect rate, work in progress, delivery reliability and cost per good unit.

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: Separate removal of waste from removal of capacity that protects a service promise.

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: Review whether the gain is sustainable after training, supplier and maintenance costs.

fragments.label: Implement lean without removing necessary resilience
fragments.text: An annual buffer costs $18,000 to hold. A supply interruption is estimated to have a 30% annual probability and cost $90,000, giving an expected disruption cost of $27,000. The simple comparison supports a buffer, but managers should challenge the probability, determine whether the stock covers the actual interruption and consider dual sourcing before deciding.
Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Construct an activity-on-arrow network from an activity table. First list every activity, its duration and its immediate predecessor or predecessors. Draw a start event, then draw one activity arrow for each task from its start event to its finish event; the arrow's direction shows sequence, not physical distance. Add a zero-duration dummy only when it is needed to preserve a dependency. Check that no activity is omitted, no two real activities have the same start and finish nodes, and no loop runs back to an earlier event. Number each node from left to right in the direction of the arrows after the logic is correct.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: A node is an event rather than a task. Record the earliest event time (EET) and latest event time (LET) at each node. For the forward pass, set the start EET to zero and use the maximum of all incoming completion times at a merge because every predecessor must finish. For the backward pass, set the final LET equal to the project duration and use the minimum of all outgoing permitted start times at a burst so no successor is delayed.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: An activity's total float shows the delay possible without extending the project. Free float is stricter: it shows delay possible without moving the earliest start of the next activity. Activities with zero total float form the critical path. Managers monitor these activities closely because a delay, unless recovered elsewhere on the critical path, delays the project.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: A dummy activity has no duration or resource. It prevents the diagram from falsely showing that an activity has the wrong predecessor; it is a logic device, not work to schedule.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Construction order: activity table → dependency arrows → necessary dummy arrows → node numbers → forward pass → backward pass → float and critical path.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Forward pass: earliest finish = earliest start + duration; use the greatest incoming value at a merge.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Backward pass: latest start = latest finish - duration; use the smallest outgoing value at a burst.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Total float = LFT at end node - EST at start node - activity duration.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Free float = EST at next node - EST at start node - activity duration.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Critical activities have zero total float; the final earliest time is the minimum project duration.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Activities are A = 3 days followed by C = 5 days; B = 4 days followed by D = 2 days; both branches must finish before E = 3 days. Route A-C-E = 3 + 5 + 3 = 11 days. Route B-D-E = 4 + 2 + 3 = 9 days. Therefore the critical path is A-C-E and the minimum project duration is 11 days.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: A: ES 0, EF 3, LS 0, LF 3, total float 0. B: ES 0, EF 4, LS 2, LF 6, total float 2. C: ES 3, EF 8, LS 3, LF 8, total float 0. D: ES 4, EF 6, LS 6, LF 8, total float 2. E: ES 8, EF 11, LS 8, LF 11, total float 0. At the merge, E cannot start until day 8 because C finishes later than D.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: For B, total float = 6 - 0 - 4 = 2 days, but free float = 4 - 0 - 4 = 0 because D begins as early as day 4. For D, total float = 8 - 4 - 2 = 2 days and free float = 8 - 4 - 2 = 2 days. Delaying A, C or E delays project completion because each is critical; delaying D by up to two days does not.

fragments.label: Critical Path Analysis: full construction and calculation
fragments.text: Suppose C needs A only, while D needs both A and B. A is 1 → 2 (3 days) and B is 1 → 3 (4 days). A dummy activity 2 → 3 has zero-day duration. C is 2 → 4 (5 days), so C begins after A only. D is 3 → 4 (2 days), so D begins after both A and B because node 3 cannot occur until B and the dummy from A are complete. Without the dummy, merging A and B before C would falsely make C depend on B; starting D directly after B would wrongly omit its dependence on A. The forward and backward passes give node 1: EET 0, LET 0. Node 2: EET 3, LET 3. Node 3: EET 4, LET 6. Node 4: EET 8, LET 8. The network duration is 8 days and A-C is the critical path.
Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: CPA makes sequence and dependence visible, identifies minimum duration and focuses management attention on critical tasks. Float supports resource allocation: labour or equipment may be moved temporarily from a non-critical activity without delaying the project, provided the remaining float and knock-on effects are checked. Alternative plans can be modelled before work begins.

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: The answer must also challenge the model. Duration estimates may be optimistic; one delayed activity can change the critical path; CPA does not by itself guarantee that the assumed employees, finance or materials are available; and a large changing project can become difficult to update. Shortening a critical task may require costly overtime or create a quality or safety problem.

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: Managers should update actual durations, recalculate the network after major changes and combine CPA with budgets, responsibility, risk registers and quality controls. The final judgement depends on estimate reliability, project complexity, the cost of delay and the organisation's ability to act on the information.

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: A critical path is a management priority, not proof that every non-critical activity can be ignored.

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: Using float consumes contingency; once used, later disruption becomes more dangerous.

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: Crashing a project is rational only when the value of earlier completion exceeds the extra cost and risk.

fragments.label: Use CPA to manage resources, not to pretend uncertainty is gone
fragments.text: In the 11-day network, the manager might move a specialist from D to C because D has two days of total float and C is critical. Before doing so, the manager must check that D still starts and finishes within its allowed times and that the specialist can actually shorten C without compromising quality.
What three forms of flexibility are on the syllabus?

fragments.label: What three forms of flexibility are on the syllabus?
fragments.text: Volume, delivery-time and specification flexibility.
Why can ERP improve inventory decisions?

fragments.label: Why can ERP improve inventory decisions?
fragments.text: Purchasing, sales and production use shared current data, reducing duplicate orders and revealing shortages sooner—if the data are accurate.
Name six lean methods in the syllabus.

fragments.label: Name six lean methods in the syllabus.
fragments.text: Kaizen, quality circles, simultaneous engineering, cell production, JIT and waste management.
What is the critical path in the worked network?

fragments.label: What is the critical path in the worked network?
fragments.text: A-C-E, with a minimum duration of 11 days.
What are B's total and free float?

fragments.label: What are B's total and free float?
fragments.text: Total float is 2 days; free float is 0 days.
What are D's total and free float?

fragments.label: What are D's total and free float?
fragments.text: Both are 2 days.
Why is a dummy activity used?

fragments.label: Why is a dummy activity used?
fragments.text: To show the correct dependency in the network; it uses no time or resource.
What do a node and an activity arrow show?

fragments.label: What do a node and an activity arrow show?
fragments.text: A node is a start or finish event; an activity arrow is a task whose direction shows dependency and whose label gives its duration.
How are event times selected at merges and bursts?

fragments.label: How are event times selected at merges and bursts?
fragments.text: Use the maximum incoming completion time for the forward-pass EET and the minimum outgoing permitted time for the backward-pass LET.
Why is CPA not sufficient by itself?

fragments.label: Why is CPA not sufficient by itself?
fragments.text: Durations are estimates and the network does not automatically solve resource, finance, quality or risk constraints.

Financial statements turn transactions into evidence about performance over a period and financial position at one date. Cambridge does not require candidates to prepare a complete set of accounts, but it does require confident amendment, calculation and interpretation: trace each change through profit, retained earnings, assets, liabilities and equity, then explain the business consequence.

fragments.label: Revenue
fragments.text: Income earned from normal sales during the accounting period, whether or not all customers have paid cash yet.

fragments.label: Cost of sales
fragments.text: The direct cost of the goods or services sold during the period.

fragments.label: Gross profit
fragments.text: Revenue minus cost of sales; evidence about pricing and direct-cost control before operating expenses.

fragments.label: Profit from operations
fragments.text: Gross profit minus operating expenses; also called operating profit in the syllabus formula appendix.

fragments.label: Net current assets
fragments.text: Current assets minus current liabilities, showing the accounting working-capital position at the reporting date.

fragments.label: Net assets
fragments.text: Total assets minus total liabilities; under the accounting equation this equals owners' equity.

fragments.label: Equity
fragments.text: Owners' long-term claim on net assets, including issued share capital and reserves.

fragments.label: Retained earnings
fragments.text: Accumulated profit kept in the business after taxation and dividends rather than distributed to owners.

fragments.label: Net realisable value
fragments.text: Expected selling value of inventory minus further costs needed to complete and sell it.

fragments.label: Depreciation
fragments.text: The annual allocation of a non-current asset's depreciable amount over its estimated useful life.

fragments.label: Carrying value
fragments.text: The cost of a non-current asset minus accumulated depreciation shown in the statement of financial position.
Statement of profit or loss: the performance story

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss: the performance story
fragments.text: The statement covers a period. Its sequence is revenue - cost of sales = gross profit; gross profit - operating expenses = profit from operations; after finance items and taxation comes profit for the year; after dividends, the balance retained can strengthen reserves. Each subtotal answers a different question, so never call every result simply 'profit'.

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss: the performance story
fragments.text: A change must be followed through. A higher selling price may raise revenue and gross profit only if volume does not fall enough. Higher material cost raises cost of sales and reduces both gross and operating profit. Higher administration cost leaves gross profit unchanged but reduces profit from operations.

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss: the performance story
fragments.text: Use the stated period and currency units before calculating.

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss: the performance story
fragments.text: Credit sales enter revenue before the cash may arrive, so profit is not the bank balance.

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss: the performance story
fragments.text: Taxation and dividends occur after operating profit; dividends are a distribution of profit, not an operating expense.

fragments.label: Statement of profit or loss: the performance story
fragments.text: Revenue $800,000 - cost of sales $500,000 = gross profit $300,000. Operating expenses of $190,000 give profit from operations = $300,000 - $190,000 = $110,000. If energy expense rises by $15,000, revised operating profit = $95,000. The $15,000 fall reduces the buffer for interest, taxation, dividends and reinvestment.
Statement of financial position: resources and financing

fragments.label: Statement of financial position: resources and financing
fragments.text: The statement is a snapshot at one date. Non-current assets support more than one period. Current assets include inventory, trade receivables and cash. Current liabilities are due within the short term; net current assets equal current assets minus current liabilities. Equity contains issued shares and reserves.

fragments.label: Statement of financial position: resources and financing
fragments.text: The accounting equation links the two sides: assets are financed by liabilities and equity. A large asset base is not proof of liquidity because premises or machinery cannot normally pay tomorrow's supplier bill.

fragments.label: Statement of financial position: resources and financing
fragments.text: A bank loan received increases cash and liabilities; it does not create profit.

fragments.label: Statement of financial position: resources and financing
fragments.text: Buying machinery for cash changes the mix of assets immediately, then depreciation affects later profit and carrying value.

fragments.label: Statement of financial position: resources and financing
fragments.text: Net current assets can be positive while cash is weak if inventory is obsolete or receivables are slow.

fragments.label: Statement of financial position: resources and financing
fragments.text: Inventory $70,000 + receivables $55,000 + cash $15,000 = current assets $140,000. Current liabilities are $95,000. Net current assets = $140,000 - $95,000 = $45,000. Separately, total assets of $600,000 minus total liabilities of $220,000 gives net assets = $380,000, which equals owners' equity. The positive $45,000 working-capital position does not remove liquidity risk because $125,000 is tied up in inventory and receivables.
How the two statements connect

fragments.label: How the two statements connect
fragments.text: Profit retained during the period adds to reserves/equity, but the cash effect depends on credit timing and other transactions. Depreciation reduces operating profit and the asset's carrying value. An inventory write-down raises cost of sales or records a loss, reducing profit, while also reducing current assets. Dividends reduce retained earnings and cash when paid.

fragments.label: How the two statements connect
fragments.text: State the line affected in the statement of profit or loss, the line affected in the statement of financial position and the decision consequence.

fragments.label: How the two statements connect
fragments.text: Higher closing inventory can raise reported profit by reducing cost of sales, but only if the valuation is recoverable.

fragments.label: How the two statements connect
fragments.text: A profitable period can still end with less cash after asset purchases, debt repayment, dividends or slower customer payment.

fragments.label: How the two statements connect
fragments.text: A depreciation charge is non-cash in the current period, but the original asset purchase was a cash investment.

fragments.label: How the two statements connect
fragments.text: A $12,000 inventory write-down reduces inventory/current assets by $12,000 and reduces profit for the year by $12,000. Lower profit then reduces retained earnings. Managers should investigate damage, obsolescence or weak demand rather than treating the accounting adjustment as the original cause.
Inventory valuation and net realisable value

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and net realisable value
fragments.text: Inventory is difficult to value when items are damaged, obsolete, unfinished, customised or subject to falling prices. Net realisable value (NRV) asks what can actually be recovered: expected selling price minus completion and selling costs. If NRV is below recorded cost, using the lower recoverable figure avoids overstating current assets and profit.

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and net realisable value
fragments.text: NRV still depends on estimates. Evidence should include recent selling prices, defect rates, disposal cost, demand and product age.

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and net realisable value
fragments.text: Do not subtract costs already incurred again; deduct future costs needed to complete and sell.

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and net realisable value
fragments.text: A write-down changes reported figures but does not itself create an immediate cash outflow.

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and net realisable value
fragments.text: Overvaluation can make liquidity and profitability appear stronger than reality.

fragments.label: Inventory valuation and net realisable value
fragments.text: An item cost $45. Expected selling price is $50, but completion and selling cost is $12. Net realisable value = $50 - $12 = $38 per item. Because $38 is below the $45 recorded cost, value inventory at $38. The $7 write-down per item lowers inventory/current assets and reported profit.
Straight-line depreciation

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Straight-line depreciation spreads cost minus expected residual value equally over estimated useful life. The annual expense reduces profit from operations. Accumulated depreciation reduces the asset's carrying value. There is no cash payment when the annual charge is recorded.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Useful life and residual value are estimates. A shorter useful life or lower residual value increases annual depreciation and lowers current reported profit. Comparisons are weaker when policies or asset ages differ.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Depreciable amount = original cost - residual value.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Carrying value after n years = cost - accumulated depreciation, subject to not falling below residual value.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: Depreciation matches asset use with the periods benefiting, but it does not create a replacement fund.

fragments.label: Straight-line depreciation
fragments.text: A machine costs $120,000, has residual value $20,000 and useful life 5 years. Annual depreciation = ($120,000 - $20,000) / 5 = $20,000 per year. After two years, carrying value = $120,000 - (2 x $20,000) = $80,000. Each annual $20,000 charge lowers profit and asset value but is not a current cash outflow.
Amending figures without losing the meaning

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: For an amendment, identify the transaction, decide whether it affects performance, position or both, recalculate the relevant subtotal and state the consequence. Avoid rebuilding irrelevant lines. A depreciation revision or inventory write-down reduces profit; a new loan increases cash and non-current liabilities but only later interest affects profit.

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: An accrual records an expense already incurred but not yet paid, increasing the period's expense and a current liability. A prepayment is cash paid for a future period: remove that amount from the current period's expense and record a current asset. Both adjustments match expense to the period receiving the benefit.

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: Show each subtotal to protect follow-through marks. A visible method demonstrates correct classification even if one arithmetic result is wrong.

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: Label whether the result is dollars, a reporting date or an annual figure.

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: Do not treat the purchase of a non-current asset as the whole year's operating expense.

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: Check that assets remain consistent with liabilities plus equity after an amendment.

fragments.label: Amending figures without losing the meaning
fragments.text: Classify -> calculate -> trace -> interpret. A $9,000 higher depreciation charge reduces operating profit, retained earnings and non-current asset carrying value by $9,000; it may worsen profitability ratios but does not directly reduce this year's cash.
Using statements for decisions

fragments.label: Using statements for decisions
fragments.text: Managers use margins, working capital, assets and financing to diagnose where strategy may need to change. Lenders look for repayment capacity and security; investors consider profitability, growth, dividends and risk; suppliers consider short-term payment evidence. The same number can lead stakeholders to different questions.

fragments.label: Using statements for decisions
fragments.text: Statements are historical and partly estimated. Combine them with cash-flow forecasts, ratios, budgets, market demand, employee capability, capacity, environmental impact and objectives.

fragments.label: Using statements for decisions
fragments.text: A fall in operating profit may justify cost diagnosis, not an automatic across-the-board cut.

fragments.label: Using statements for decisions
fragments.text: Rising assets after investment are positive only if utilisation and future returns are credible.

fragments.label: Using statements for decisions
fragments.text: A judgement should identify the decision, evidence, limitation and further information needed.

fragments.label: Using statements for decisions
fragments.text: Operating profit falls while receivables rise. One hypothesis is weaker credit control: cash arrives later and bad-debt risk rises. Before tightening terms, compare customer mix, sales growth, overdue age and competitor terms because strict collection could lose valuable customers.
What is the sequence from revenue to operating profit?

fragments.label: What is the sequence from revenue to operating profit?
fragments.text: Revenue - cost of sales = gross profit; gross profit - operating expenses = profit from operations.
Why can profit rise before cash?

fragments.label: Why can profit rise before cash?
fragments.text: Credit sales enter revenue when earned, while customer cash may arrive later.
How is NRV calculated?

fragments.label: How is NRV calculated?
fragments.text: Expected selling price minus further costs needed to complete and sell inventory.
What does an inventory write-down affect?

fragments.label: What does an inventory write-down affect?
fragments.text: It reduces inventory/current assets and profit, which also reduces retained earnings.
How is straight-line depreciation calculated?

fragments.label: How is straight-line depreciation calculated?
fragments.text: Cost minus residual value, divided by useful life.
Does depreciation directly reduce current cash?

fragments.label: Does depreciation directly reduce current cash?
fragments.text: No. It is an accounting allocation; the asset purchase caused the cash outflow.
Why is a statement of financial position a snapshot?

fragments.label: Why is a statement of financial position a snapshot?
fragments.text: It reports assets, liabilities and equity at one specific date.

Ratios compress financial statements into signals about liquidity, profitability, financial efficiency, gearing and investor return. A calculation earns only the start of an answer. The examiner-ready method is calculate accurately, compare with a meaningful benchmark, diagnose plausible causes, trace business consequences, propose a contextual response and evaluate the evidence limits.

fragments.label: Liquidity
fragments.text: Ability to meet short-term obligations when they fall due.

fragments.label: Profitability
fragments.text: Ability to generate profit relative to revenue or long-term capital used.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency
fragments.text: How effectively inventory, receivables, payables and capital are managed to support performance.

fragments.label: Capital employed
fragments.text: Issued shares plus reserves plus non-current liabilities under the Cambridge formula appendix.

fragments.label: Gearing
fragments.text: The proportion of capital employed financed by non-current liabilities.

fragments.label: Earnings per share
fragments.text: Profit attributable to each ordinary share; used as the denominator of the price/earnings ratio.

fragments.label: Dividend yield
fragments.text: Dividend per share as a percentage of market price per share.

fragments.label: Dividend cover
fragments.text: How many times profit for the year covers the annual dividend.

fragments.label: Price/earnings ratio
fragments.text: Market price per share divided by earnings per share, reflecting how highly the market values current earnings.

fragments.label: Window dressing
fragments.text: Actions or presentation around the reporting date that make reported position appear temporarily stronger.
Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios

fragments.label: Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios
fragments.text: Current ratio compares all current assets with current liabilities. Acid test removes inventory because it may take time to sell, may be obsolete or may realise less than its recorded value. Low liquidity can delay payments and disrupt supply; extremely high liquidity can indicate idle cash, excessive inventory or weak receivables collection.

fragments.label: Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios
fragments.text: There is no universal ideal. Supermarkets may operate with low ratios because customers pay immediately while suppliers allow credit. A seasonal manufacturer may need a larger buffer. Interpret trend, cash conversion, access to finance and the timing of liabilities.

fragments.label: Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios
fragments.text: Possible improvements: collect receivables faster, reduce suitable inventory, negotiate supplier credit, refinance short debt or inject long-term finance.

fragments.label: Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios
fragments.text: A short-term loan that adds equal cash and current liability may not solve the underlying cycle.

fragments.label: Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios
fragments.text: Do not claim a ratio below 1 always means failure or a high ratio always means strength.

fragments.label: Liquidity: current and acid-test ratios
fragments.text: Current assets $180,000; inventory $60,000; current liabilities $120,000. Current ratio = $180,000 / $120,000 = 1.5 : 1. Acid-test ratio = ($180,000 - $60,000) / $120,000 = 1.0 : 1. The business has $1.50 of current assets per $1 of short-term liabilities, but only $1.00 after inventory is removed; compare collection timing and supplier terms before judging liquidity.
Profitability: margins and ROCE

fragments.label: Profitability: margins and ROCE
fragments.text: Gross profit margin reflects selling price, sales mix and cost of sales. Operating profit margin also captures operating expenses such as administration and distribution. ROCE compares profit from operations with long-term finance committed, so it asks whether the business uses capital productively.

fragments.label: Profitability: margins and ROCE
fragments.text: Diagnose the gap. If gross margin falls but operating margin falls by the same amount, direct costs or price may dominate. If gross margin is stable while operating margin falls, overhead growth is more likely. ROCE can fall after investment before the new capacity generates profit.

fragments.label: Profitability: margins and ROCE
fragments.text: Improve a margin through price, mix, purchasing, productivity or waste reduction only if demand, quality and capacity consequences are acceptable.

fragments.label: Profitability: margins and ROCE
fragments.text: Compare ROCE with prior years, competitors, objectives and finance cost, using consistent accounting policies.

fragments.label: Profitability: margins and ROCE
fragments.text: Revenue growth with a falling margin may still raise absolute profit; calculate rather than assume.

fragments.label: Profitability: margins and ROCE
fragments.text: Revenue $1,000,000; gross profit $360,000; profit from operations $120,000; capital employed $800,000. Gross profit margin = $360,000 / $1,000,000 x 100 = 36%. Operating profit margin = $120,000 / $1,000,000 x 100 = 12%. ROCE = $120,000 / $800,000 x 100 = 15%. The 24 percentage-point gap between gross and operating margins directs attention to operating expenses; 15% ROCE needs a trend and finance-cost benchmark.
Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: Rate of inventory turnover shows how many times average inventory is sold or used during the period. Receivables days estimates average customer collection time using credit sales. Payables days estimates average supplier payment time using credit purchases. Use the exact credit figure when provided rather than total revenue or purchases.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: Direction is contextual. Faster inventory turnover can release cash but may cause stockouts. Fewer receivables days improves cash but strict terms may lose customers. More payables days preserves cash but may lose discounts, trust or supply.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: Compare days with stated credit terms and aged balances, not just last year.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: Inventory turnover varies by product: food and luxury machinery cannot share one benchmark.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: A change may be caused by sales mix, purchasing, disruption or accounting cut-off as well as management efficiency.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: Cost of sales is $600,000 and average inventory is $100,000. Rate of inventory turnover = $600,000 / $100,000 = 6 times per year. If the competitor turns stock 9 times, the business may hold slow inventory, but product mix and service-buffer needs must be checked before reducing stock.

fragments.label: Financial efficiency: inventory, receivables and payables
fragments.text: Trade receivables $75,000 and credit sales $750,000 give receivables days = $75,000 / $750,000 x 365 = 36.5 days. Trade payables $48,000 and credit purchases $438,000 give payables days = $48,000 / $438,000 x 365 = 40 days. Cash is collected before suppliers are paid on average, but overdue customer concentration and supplier terms still matter.
Gearing and financial risk

fragments.label: Gearing and financial risk
fragments.text: Cambridge gearing is non-current liabilities divided by capital employed. Higher gearing means more fixed interest and repayment exposure. It can magnify owner returns when operating return exceeds debt cost, preserve control and fund growth, but it reduces resilience when cash flow is volatile or rates rise.

fragments.label: Gearing and financial risk
fragments.text: The percentage needs context. A utility with predictable cash may sustain debt that would be dangerous for a start-up. Evaluate interest cover/cash evidence when available, asset security, maturity, rate structure and how the borrowed funds will be used.

fragments.label: Gearing and financial risk
fragments.text: Debt-financed growth usually raises gearing initially; retained profit or new equity can lower it.

fragments.label: Gearing and financial risk
fragments.text: Paying debt with scarce cash may improve gearing but weaken liquidity.

fragments.label: Gearing and financial risk
fragments.text: A figure over 50% signals more debt than equity under this formula, not automatic insolvency.

fragments.label: Gearing and financial risk
fragments.text: Non-current liabilities $300,000; issued shares $250,000; reserves $200,000. Capital employed = $250,000 + $200,000 + $300,000 = $750,000. Gearing = $300,000 / $750,000 x 100 = 40%. Borrowing another $150,000 would raise debt and interest risk; judge it against expected project cash flow and the current 40% base.
Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover

fragments.label: Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover
fragments.text: Price/earnings compares market price with earnings per share. A high P/E may signal growth expectations or overvaluation; a low P/E may signal weak expectations or an overlooked opportunity. Dividend yield measures current cash return relative to share price. Dividend cover measures how safely profit supports the payout and how much is retained.

fragments.label: Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover
fragments.text: Investor objectives differ. Income investors may value yield and stability; growth investors may accept low dividends if retained earnings fund positive investments. Market price is affected by external sentiment and expectations, so management cannot control every movement.

fragments.label: Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover
fragments.text: Use profit for the year / annual dividend for Cambridge dividend cover.

fragments.label: Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover
fragments.text: Higher dividends raise payout now but lower cover and retained finance, all else equal.

fragments.label: Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover
fragments.text: A falling share price mechanically raises dividend yield if dividend is unchanged; that is not necessarily good news.

fragments.label: Investor return: P/E, dividend yield and dividend cover
fragments.text: Market price $4.00; earnings per share $0.40; dividend per share $0.16; profit for year $2,000,000; annual dividend $800,000. P/E = $4.00 / $0.40 = 10 times. Dividend yield = $0.16 / $4.00 x 100 = 4%. Dividend cover = $2,000,000 / $800,000 = 2.5 times. The payout has a profit buffer, but investor appeal depends on growth, risk and alternative returns.
From ratio to comparative diagnosis

fragments.label: From ratio to comparative diagnosis
fragments.text: Use a disciplined chain: result -> direction -> benchmark -> plausible cause -> consequence -> response -> qualification. A trend shows change but not cause. A competitor benchmark adds perspective but only when industry, size, product mix and accounting policies are comparable.

fragments.label: From ratio to comparative diagnosis
fragments.text: Use ratios together. Falling operating margin, slower receivables and higher gearing can connect: weak cost control and delayed cash increase borrowing, which raises risk. One ratio alone could support several explanations.

fragments.label: From ratio to comparative diagnosis
fragments.text: Quantify change in percentage points where comparing percentages; do not call it a percent change unless calculated.

fragments.label: From ratio to comparative diagnosis
fragments.text: Name evidence from the case before proposing a cause.

fragments.label: From ratio to comparative diagnosis
fragments.text: Recommend a response only after diagnosing whether price, volume, cost, working capital or financing is driving the result.

fragments.label: From ratio to comparative diagnosis
fragments.text: Operating margin falls from 14% to 9%, receivables days rise from 32 to 51 and gearing rises from 35% to 55%. Slower collection may have created a cash gap financed by debt while higher operating costs reduced margin. Tighten credit selectively and diagnose expenses before more borrowing; test whether rapid sales growth explains some of the working-capital strain.
Improving ratios without damaging the business

fragments.label: Improving ratios without damaging the business
fragments.text: A ratio target can create perverse action. Cutting inventory improves liquidity and turnover only until shortages lose sales. Delaying suppliers improves short-term cash but may remove discounts or reliability. Raising price improves margins only if lost volume and competitor response do not outweigh the gain.

fragments.label: Improving ratios without damaging the business
fragments.text: Choose a policy bundle linked to the diagnosed cause, assign a metric and time horizon, and monitor stakeholder effects. Sustainable performance matters more than cosmetically improving the reporting-date number.

fragments.label: Improving ratios without damaging the business
fragments.text: Liquidity: credit control, inventory design, supplier negotiation and suitable long-term finance.

fragments.label: Improving ratios without damaging the business
fragments.text: Profitability: value-based price, product mix, purchasing, process quality and justified overhead control.

fragments.label: Improving ratios without damaging the business
fragments.text: Investor return: profitable investment, appropriate dividends, risk control and credible communication.

fragments.label: Improving ratios without damaging the business
fragments.text: Pressuring every customer to pay immediately may reduce receivables days, but a large business buyer could switch supplier. Segment overdue/high-risk accounts, preserve justified strategic credit and track cash collected, bad debt and customer retention.
Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis
fragments.text: Published figures are historical, may be months old, use estimates and accounting policies, and can be distorted by inflation, one-off items, acquisitions, seasonal reporting dates and window dressing. Intangible strengths such as skills, innovation, culture, brand and customer loyalty are incompletely recorded.

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis
fragments.text: Ratios reveal symptoms, not proven causes. Cross-company comparison can fail where product mix, geography, accounting year, asset age or policy differs. Use notes to accounts, narrative reports, cash forecasts and operational/market evidence before deciding.

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis
fragments.text: Audited does not mean every forecast or strategic claim is guaranteed.

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis
fragments.text: Averages can hide a single overdue customer or obsolete inventory category.

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis
fragments.text: External conditions can change after year end, so current evidence matters.

fragments.label: Limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis
fragments.text: A retailer and manufacturer both report current ratio 1.2:1. The retailer may collect cash immediately and turn stock quickly, while the manufacturer waits months for customers. The identical ratio therefore does not imply identical liquidity risk.
Why does acid test remove inventory?

fragments.label: Why does acid test remove inventory?
fragments.text: Inventory may be slower or less certain to convert into cash than other current assets.
What is Cambridge capital employed?

fragments.label: What is Cambridge capital employed?
fragments.text: Issued shares plus reserves plus non-current liabilities.
What does a falling gross margin direct you to investigate?

fragments.label: What does a falling gross margin direct you to investigate?
fragments.text: Selling price, product mix and cost of sales before operating expenses.
Why are lower receivables days not automatically best?

fragments.label: Why are lower receivables days not automatically best?
fragments.text: Strict credit may improve cash but lose valuable customers or sales.
What does gearing measure?

fragments.label: What does gearing measure?
fragments.text: Non-current liabilities as a percentage of capital employed.
How can dividend yield rise for a negative reason?

fragments.label: How can dividend yield rise for a negative reason?
fragments.text: An unchanged dividend divided by a falling share price produces a higher yield.
What is the ratio-analysis answer chain?

fragments.label: What is the ratio-analysis answer chain?
fragments.text: Calculate, compare, diagnose, explain consequence, recommend and qualify.

Investment appraisal tests whether a long-term project fits a business's liquidity, return and value objectives. Payback, Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) and Net Present Value (NPV) answer different questions, so the strongest recommendation calculates all available evidence, explains conflicting rankings and integrates forecast risk, strategic fit and stakeholder effects.

fragments.label: Investment appraisal
fragments.text: Quantitative and qualitative assessment of a long-term capital project before resources are committed.

fragments.label: Net cash flow
fragments.text: Cash inflow minus cash outflow for a period; used by payback and NPV.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Time required for cumulative net cash inflows to recover the initial investment.

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: Average annual accounting profit as a percentage of average investment.

fragments.label: Average investment
fragments.text: The average capital tied up, commonly (initial investment plus residual value) divided by two when the question supplies those figures.

fragments.label: Discount factor
fragments.text: Multiplier that converts a future cash flow into present value at a stated discount rate.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Total present value of future net cash flows minus initial investment.

fragments.label: Time value of money
fragments.text: Money received now is worth more than the same nominal amount later because it can earn a return and future receipt is uncertain.
Why investment appraisal is needed

fragments.label: Why investment appraisal is needed
fragments.text: Capital projects consume scarce finance, affect capacity and cost for years and may be difficult to reverse. Appraisal compares liquidity speed, accounting return and value after recognising timing. It supports prioritisation, lending discussions and post-investment targets.

fragments.label: Why investment appraisal is needed
fragments.text: A model does not remove uncertainty. Demand, price, operating cost, project life, residual value and discount rate are forecasts. Managers should use sensitivity or scenarios and identify which assumption would reverse the decision.

fragments.label: Why investment appraisal is needed
fragments.text: Use incremental project cash flows, not total business sales.

fragments.label: Why investment appraisal is needed
fragments.text: Keep cash flows for payback/NPV separate from accounting profit for ARR.

fragments.label: Why investment appraisal is needed
fragments.text: Compare results with the firm's target payback, target ARR and required return where provided.

fragments.label: Why investment appraisal is needed
fragments.text: A cash-constrained technology firm may prioritise payback because obsolescence and liquidity risk are high. A financially secure firm comparing long-lived projects may place more weight on positive NPV and strategic capacity. Neither criterion is automatically best without the objective and constraint.
Payback period

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: List annual net cash inflows and accumulate them until they recover initial cost. If recovery occurs during a year and flows are assumed even, divide the amount still unrecovered at the start of that year by that year's inflow. State years and months or a decimal year.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Short payback reduces the time cash is exposed and can help liquidity, especially where technology or demand changes quickly. It ignores cash flows after payback and usually ignores time value, so it cannot measure total profitability or value.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Decision rule: accept if payback is within the target, or prefer the shorter payback if all else is comparable.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Subtract each year's net cash flow from the unrecovered balance to avoid cumulative errors.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: A project paying back quickly can still have low lifetime return.

fragments.label: Payback period
fragments.text: Initial investment $100,000. Net cash inflows are $40,000 in year 1, $40,000 in year 2 and $40,000 in year 3. After year 2, $80,000 has been recovered, leaving $20,000. Fraction of year 3 = $20,000 / $40,000 = 0.5 year. Payback = 2.5 years. This meets a 3-year target and limits liquidity exposure, but later cash flows still matter.
Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: ARR uses average annual accounting profit, not cash flow. Find total accounting profit across the project, divide by project life, then divide by average investment and multiply by 100. Under the standard convention, average investment is (initial investment + residual value) / 2; follow any convention explicitly specified in the question.

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: ARR provides a percentage familiar for targets and comparison and considers profit across the life. It ignores when profit occurs, depends on depreciation and accounting estimates, and may be inconsistent where conventions differ.

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: Decision rule: accept if ARR exceeds the target or finance benchmark, subject to risk and strategy.

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: Do not put total cash inflow or revenue in the numerator.

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: Show the average-profit and average-investment stages before the percentage.

fragments.label: Accounting Rate of Return (ARR)
fragments.text: Initial investment $180,000; residual value $20,000; project life 4 years; total accounting profit $100,000. Average annual profit = $100,000 / 4 = $25,000 per year. Average investment = ($180,000 + $20,000) / 2 = $100,000. ARR = $25,000 / $100,000 x 100 = 25%. It exceeds a 20% target, so it passes the accounting-return test, but timing and forecast risk still need evaluation.
Net Present Value (NPV)

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Multiply each future net cash flow by its supplied discount factor to find present value. Add the present values and subtract the initial investment. Positive NPV means the discounted inflows exceed cost at the chosen discount rate; negative NPV fails that financial test. When projects are mutually exclusive and comparable, higher positive NPV adds more forecast value.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: NPV recognises timing and all project cash flows, but depends on the accuracy of flows, life and discount rate. A single rate may not capture project-specific risk, inflation or changing finance conditions.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Decision rule: financially accept NPV greater than zero at the required rate.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Use the table's discount factors; do not add undiscounted and discounted figures together.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Keep the initial investment as a time-zero outflow and show its negative sign.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: The discounted year 1-5 net cash flows total $132,000 and initial investment is $120,000. NPV = $132,000 - $120,000 = +$12,000. The positive $12,000 means the project is financially acceptable at the stated discount rate and is forecast to add present value. Accept only if the cash-flow assumptions, risk and strategic fit are credible.

fragments.label: Net Present Value (NPV)
fragments.text: Formula: present value = net cash flow × discount factor. Year 1: $50,000 × 0.909 = $45,450 present value. Year 2: $70,000 × 0.826 = $57,820 present value. Total present value = $45,450 + $57,820 = $103,270. With an initial investment of $90,000, NPV = $103,270 − $90,000 = +$13,270. The positive $13,270 is financially acceptable at the stated discount rate, subject to cash-flow and risk assumptions.
When the methods disagree

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: A project may pay back quickly but generate little later value, or have high NPV but slow payback. Do not average unlike measures. Explain what each method prioritises, link that priority to the business's objective and constraint, and test whether a plausible forecast change reverses the ranking.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Sensitivity can recalculate lower sales, higher operating cost, delayed launch, shorter life or a different discount rate. Focus on the assumption with the largest decision impact rather than changing every number mechanically.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Cash shortage and high uncertainty increase the relevance of payback.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Long-lived projects and shareholder-value objectives increase the relevance of NPV.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Management targets may use ARR, but accounting policy can affect comparison.

fragments.label: When the methods disagree
fragments.text: Project A pays back in 2.2 years with NPV $30,000; Project B pays back in 3.6 years with NPV $85,000. A may suit severe liquidity or obsolescence risk; B may add more value for a well-financed firm. Recalculate B under delayed cash inflows before recommending it.
Qualitative and strategic judgement

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: Consider alignment with objectives, product/market strategy, capacity bottlenecks, quality, flexibility, skills, employee response, customer service, environmental effects, regulation, reputation, supplier dependence and competitor reaction. Availability and source of finance can constrain even a positive project.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: Forecast reliability must be tested alongside strategic fit, stakeholder effects and risk. Implementation matters: disruption, training, installation, cybersecurity, maintenance and fallback arrangements can change actual cash flows and stakeholder outcomes.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: A mandatory safety or legal investment may proceed despite a weak standalone return.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: A project with good figures may be rejected if it damages a core capability or exceeds management capacity.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: State what evidence would change the recommendation: pilot results, orders, finance rate or sensitivity threshold.

fragments.label: Qualitative and strategic judgement
fragments.text: An automated line has the highest NPV but requires scarce technicians and may interrupt delivery during installation. Phase implementation or training may protect customer contracts even if it slightly lowers the numerical return.
Building the recommendation

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Start with the verified calculation and decision rule. Compare the competing method, then develop one project-specific benefit and one risk to cash, profit, objective or stakeholder. Finish with a conditional judgement stating the decisive criterion and assumption.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Official schemes separate calculation from evaluation: accurate figures do not by themselves justify the final choice. Conversely, qualitative discussion should not ignore a clear positive or negative NPV.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Quantitative: result, unit, criterion and comparison.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Qualitative: factor, contextual mechanism and business consequence.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Judgement: objective, constraint, time horizon and reversal trigger.

fragments.label: Building the recommendation
fragments.text: Choose Project B because its +$85,000 NPV best supports long-term value and finance is available, despite slower payback; switch to A if sensitivity testing shows B's cash inflows fall enough to make NPV negative or if the firm cannot fund the 3.6-year exposure.
What does payback measure?

fragments.label: What does payback measure?
fragments.text: How long cumulative net cash inflows take to recover initial investment.
What data does ARR use?

fragments.label: What data does ARR use?
fragments.text: Average annual accounting profit divided by average investment, multiplied by 100.
What is the NPV acceptance rule?

fragments.label: What is the NPV acceptance rule?
fragments.text: NPV above zero is financially acceptable at the stated discount rate.
Why may payback and NPV rank projects differently?

fragments.label: Why may payback and NPV rank projects differently?
fragments.text: Payback prioritises recovery speed and ignores later flows, while NPV includes timing and all forecast flows.
Name three qualitative factors.

fragments.label: Name three qualitative factors.
fragments.text: Strategic fit, employee/skill impact and environmental or customer consequences; finance and implementation risk also matter.
What should sensitivity analysis identify?

fragments.label: What should sensitivity analysis identify?
fragments.text: Whether a plausible change in an important assumption reverses the decision.
Why is appraisal not a guarantee?

fragments.label: Why is appraisal not a guarantee?
fragments.text: Cash flows, project life, residual value and discount rate are forecasts or assumptions.

Finance strategy connects accounting evidence to long-term choices about investment, working capital, debt, equity, dividends and growth. The goal is not to improve a ratio cosmetically: it is to choose a coherent policy that supports corporate objectives while keeping liquidity, return, control, risk and stakeholder consequences within acceptable limits.

fragments.label: Finance strategy
fragments.text: Long-term approach to acquiring, allocating and controlling finance so corporate objectives can be achieved at acceptable risk.

fragments.label: Annual report
fragments.text: Package containing financial statements and narrative, governance, risk, sustainability and other information for stakeholders.

fragments.label: Audit opinion
fragments.text: Independent auditor's conclusion on whether statements meet the relevant reporting requirements; it is not a guarantee of future success.

fragments.label: Debt finance
fragments.text: Borrowed finance with contractual interest and repayment, usually preserving ownership control.

fragments.label: Equity finance
fragments.text: Owner/shareholder finance with no contractual repayment but possible dilution of ownership and earnings.

fragments.label: Dividend policy
fragments.text: Approach to distributing profit to shareholders versus retaining it for liquidity and investment.

fragments.label: Financial risk
fragments.text: Risk created by fixed finance commitments and inability to meet interest or repayment when cash flow weakens.

fragments.label: Window dressing
fragments.text: Temporary action or presentation designed to make reported position look stronger at the reporting date.
From accounting evidence to strategy

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Financial statements and ratios reveal resources, profitability, liquidity, efficiency, financing and investor return. Strategy uses that evidence to diagnose constraints and opportunities: weak liquidity may delay expansion; falling margins may require product, price, cost or process action; underused assets may support growth without major investment.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Use a sequence: objective -> evidence -> diagnosis -> option -> financial and non-financial consequence -> implementation -> control. A ratio target is not an objective by itself unless it supports survival, growth, return or another corporate aim.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Use a balanced set of ratios; improving one can worsen another.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Separate a temporary investment effect from persistent weak performance.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Attach targets, owners, time periods and review triggers to the chosen policy.

fragments.label: From accounting evidence to strategy
fragments.text: Operating margin falls while sales grow and defect returns rise. The strategy should diagnose quality and failure cost before cutting promotion or staff. Better process quality may reduce rework, improve margin and protect reputation even if training initially increases expense.
Annual reports and stakeholder decisions

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: An annual report may include the financial statements, notes, strategic or directors' report, governance, principal risks, sustainability information and an independent audit report. Notes explain accounting policies and unusual items that headline ratios can hide. Narrative sections add context but management selects how to present its story.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: Managers plan and control; investors assess return and risk; lenders assess repayment; suppliers assess payment confidence; employees consider continuity; government and communities consider compliance and impact. The same report supports different decisions.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: An unmodified audit opinion increases confidence in reporting, not certainty that strategy will succeed.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: Forward-looking statements remain assumptions and should be tested against external evidence.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: Stakeholders need information relevant to their own time horizon and exposure.

fragments.label: Annual reports and stakeholder decisions
fragments.text: A high dividend may please an income investor, while a lender may prefer retained cash and lower debt. Employees may focus on continuity and planned restructuring. A strategy answer should identify whose decision is being supported.
Debt, equity and the capital structure

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: Debt preserves ownership and interest may be predictable, but raises gearing, fixed cash commitments and covenant/security risk. Equity has no contractual repayment and can absorb uncertainty, but dilutes control and earnings per share and creates expectations of future return. Retained earnings preserve control but have opportunity cost and may be insufficient.

fragments.label: Debt, equity and the capital structure
fragments.text: Match the source to purpose and cash timing. Stable cash flows and low existing gearing can support debt; uncertain, long-payback innovation may suit equity. Compare total cost, availability, flexibility, control and downside survival, not interest alone.
